title: ESG performance and earnings management in publicly listed firms from G20 countries
summary: This study explores the connection between Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) performance and Earnings Management (EM), as well as the fact that firm age moderates the association. It is also concerned with whether ESG practices are actually good internal governance interventions or mere symbolic disclosures obscuring financial manipulation. This study uses dynamic panel data analysis on a sample of 4,884 publicly listed firms from G20 countries for the period 2013–2023 to generate 18,962 firm-year observations. EM is calculated using discretionary accruals from Jones (1991) model. ESG scores are computed from Bloomberg, and firm age is the duration since the firm’s incorporation. The findings indicate a generally negative association between ESG performance and earnings management, although the baseline effect is only marginally significant. Therefore, the evidence suggests a cautious disciplining role of ESG, which becomes clearer when firm age is considered a moderating condition. We contribute to the literature on this topic by integrating agency, stakeholder, legitimacy, and institutional theories to understand the link between ESG and EM. Firm age is presented as a new moderating variable, allowing an assessment of the heterogeneity of ESG’s impact on financial integrity over organizational life cycles. This study also presents credible evidence from accrual-based and modified models.

title: Instruments for integrating social responsibility into corporate governance of Ukrainian enterprises
summary: This article examines the tools for integrating social responsibility into the corporate governance system of Ukrainian enterprises, taking into account military risks, resource constraints, and changes in the European regulatory environment. The study aims to justify a management approach in which social responsibility is not limited to charitable initiatives and public declarations but influences strategic decisions, the distribution of authority, human resources management, procurement, and risk assessment. The methodological framework consists of systemic and institutional approaches, a comparative analysis of scholarly works by Ukrainian authors, a review of international recommendations, and structural-functional generalization. The study distinguishes corporate philanthropy, socially responsible behavior, and the management of a company’s material impacts on employees, partners, communities, and the environment. The study proposes a sequence for integrating responsibility into the management cycle, including identifying material impacts, designating responsible individuals, incorporating measures into budgets and operational processes, verifying results, and adjusting decisions. Corporate management tools are systematized by purpose, and a matrix for verifying the relevance of non-financial indicators is proposed. The study argues that managerial effectiveness in social responsibility should be assessed not by the number of measures implemented, but by the enterprise’s ability to mitigate negative impacts, fulfill obligations, and ensure transparent feedback with stakeholders. The study examines how risk-based due diligence, budgeting, and managerial accountability fit within the corporate governance system. It establishes that integrating these tools creates the conditions for aligning managerial decisions with the principles of social responsibility. The paper supports the feasibility of applying the proposed tools in enterprises of various sizes, considering their organizational and resource characteristics, without mechanically applying requirements established for large international companies. Keywords: corporate governance, corporate management, corporate social responsibility, sustainable development, risks, enterprises, business, competitiveness.

title: Digital transformation conditions and management effectiveness through digital leadership capacity in Vietnamese primary and secondary schools
summary: Digital transformation introduces organizational demands concerning school coordination, administrative decisions, and leadership capability development. This study examines associations among transformation conditions, digital leadership capacity, and perceived management effectiveness in Vietnamese schools. Responses from 585 principals and vice principals are analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. A reflective formative hierarchical model integrates managerial, institutional, and policy contextual conditions within a higher order construct. Transformation conditions are positively associated with digital leadership capacity (β = 0.545) and perceived management effectiveness (β = 0.245). Leadership capacity is positively associated with management effectiveness (β = 0.445), alongside a significant indirect association (β = 0.243). Explained variance reaches 29.7% for leadership capacity and 37.7% for perceived management effectiveness. The findings connect an enabling organizational environment with leadership capability and perceived administrative functioning across participating schools. The framework directs theoretical attention toward coordination between organizational provision and leadership practice during digital transformation. Practical priorities include reliable systems, professional learning, and structured support for implementation decisions.

title: Board monitoring and the informational content of ESG performance
summary: Purpose This study aims to examine whether improvements in environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance are associated with subsequent realised firm outcomes and whether board monitoring conditions these relationships. Using UK FTSE 350 firms, the study evaluates whether year-on-year ESG improvements predict ESG controversies, environmental incidents, investment inefficiency and future operating performance. It further investigates whether stronger board monitoring increases the extent to which ESG improvements are associated with favourable subsequent outcomes. Design/methodology/approach The study uses an unbalanced panel of 314 FTSE 350 firms, comprising 4,396 firm-year observations from 2010 to 2024, with ESG, governance and financial data from LSEG. Panel regressions include industry and year fixed effects with firm-clustered standard errors. Board monitoring is measured using a composite index based on board independence, CEO-chair role separation and board ESG expertise. Robustness tests include disaggregated governance components, an ESG measure excluding the governance pillar, firm fixed effects, lagged specifications and multicollinearity diagnostics. Findings ESG improvements are not consistently associated with subsequent ESG controversies, investment inefficiency or future operating performance. For environmental incidents, however, the interaction between ESG improvement and board monitoring is negative and statistically significant, indicating that the association becomes more favourable as monitoring strengthens. Component-level analyses show similar negative moderation for board independence, CEO-chair separation and ESG expertise, although statistical strength varies. The result also remains when the governance pillar is excluded from the ESG measure. Lagged specifications provide more limited evidence, indicating that the relationship is outcome-specific and not persistent across all time horizons. Research limitations/implications The study focuses on UK listed firms operating within a relatively strong governance environment, which may limit generalisability to weaker institutional settings. The board monitoring index uses equal weighting, although component-level tests reduce concerns regarding this construction. The outcome measures capture specific dimensions of realised firm behaviour and do not directly measure greenwashing, managerial intent or board detection processes. Future research could examine alternative governance measures, weighting schemes, outcome intensity, other institutional settings and additional mechanisms such as ownership structure, executive incentives and external assurance. Practical implications The findings suggest that ESG score improvements should not be interpreted in isolation as evidence of substantive operational change. For boards, the results highlight the importance of effective oversight in linking ESG initiatives to underlying business practices, particularly in environmentally sensitive areas. For investors, ESG changes may be more informative when considered alongside governance characteristics. For regulators and standard setters, the evidence suggests that enhanced ESG disclosure alone may be insufficient unless supported by governance structures that promote accountability and substantive implementation. Social implications The study has broader implications for corporate accountability and stakeholder confidence in ESG information. By showing that ESG improvements are not uniformly associated with realised outcomes, the findings reinforce the need for stronger governance and scrutiny over how sustainability claims relate to actual corporate behaviour. More credible alignment between ESG performance and operational conduct may improve the usefulness of sustainability information for employees, communities, investors and other stakeholders and may help reduce the risk that symbolic improvements are interpreted as evidence of substantive social or environmental progress. Originality/value The study contributes by shifting attention from ESG levels to the informational content of ESG improvements and their association with subsequent realised outcomes. It further shows that this relationship is conditional on board monitoring and differs across outcome types. Unlike studies focused mainly on ESG disclosure or contemporaneous firm value, this study links changes in ESG performance to future adverse events, investment efficiency and operating performance. It also provides new evidence that the environmental-outcome relationship is not solely driven by the construction of the composite monitoring index or mechanical overlap with the ESG governance pillar.

title: Pengaruh Financial Technology (Fintech), Literasi Keuangan, dan Perilaku Keuangan Terhadap Pengelolaan Keuangan Pribadi Generasi Muda Kota Makassar
summary: This study aims to analyze the effects of financial technology (fintech) and financial literacy on the personal financial management of young people in Makassar City, with financial behavior serving as an intervening variable. This study employed a quantitative approach with an associative research design. The research data were collected through an online questionnaire distributed to 107 young people aged 17–25 years who resided in Makassar City and had used financial technology services. The sampling technique employed was purposive sampling. Data analysis was conducted using validity tests, reliability tests, descriptive analysis, classical assumption tests, path analysis, and the Sobel test, with the assistance of statistical software. The results indicate that financial technology and financial literacy have positive and significant effects on financial behavior. Financial technology, financial literacy, and financial behavior also have positive and significant effects on personal financial management. Financial behavior was found to partially mediate the effects of both financial technology and financial literacy on personal financial management. These findings indicate that the wise utilization of financial technology, supported by sound financial literacy, can foster healthy financial behavior and thereby promote better personal financial management among young people.

title: Agentic Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning for Enterprise-Wide Intelligent Automation and Digital Transformation in Saudi Arabia under Vision 2030
summary: Enterprise automation is moving on from simple software rules to systems that can take in a request, work out what tools to use, co-ordinate a range of specialist agents and then make decisions based on the feedback they receive. That said, greater technical autonomy doesn't in itself lead to organisational change. This integrative review looks at how agentic AI, machine learning and the existing forms of process automation can be brought together to enable enterprise-wide change in Saudi Arabia as part of Vision 2030. It draws on 30 DOI identifiable publications from 2020–2025, covering the technological, organisational and Saudi specific evidence. A concept-based analytical approach is used to separate out what is actually demonstrated from what is merely proposed in terms of architecture and to assess the degree to which the findings can be applied to regulated enterprise workflows. Six interrelated dimensions are identified: process suitability, intelligent orchestration, data and infrastructure, human capability, risk governance and value measurement. The proposed architecture for accountable automation is one in which decision rights, evidence provenance and exception handling are all situated around a bounded agent execution loop. The Saudi case studies do suggest that management buy-in and digital maturity are important, but provide very little in the way of direct evidence on the scale of agentic deployment. The review therefore does not accept that agent autonomy, economic benefit and public legitimacy are equivalent. It does provide a context sensitive design framework and a testable research agenda for enterprises that are looking for real transformation that is reliable, interoperable and inclusive rather than just a series of isolated proofs of concept. Longitudinal, sector specific evaluation is required before any claim can be made about causal national outcomes.

title: A generalised equilibrium model of random dynamics: analysing the impact of artificial intelligence and digital transformation on Vietnam’s long-term economic growth
summary: This study develops an extended Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium (DSGE) model that integrates innovation, artificial intelligence (AI), and digital transformation into a macroeconomic framework for Vietnam. The model employs a parsimonious, single-channel architecture: three forms of rival capital (physical, digital, and AI) enter a single production function, while a non-rival knowledge stock drives endogenous total factor productivity. Calibrated using Vietnamese aggregate evidence and policy anchors for 2000–2024, supplemented by international proxy ranges, the model shows that sustained, institutionally supported investment in AI and digital transformation can raise long-run output and welfare. The magnitude of these conditional gains is moderate and depends strongly on institutional quality and public spending, while remaining quantitatively sensitive to selected knowledge and policy parameters. Artificial intelligence (AI) and digital transformation offer opportunities to improve productivity and living standards in Vietnam. Using an economic model calibrated to Vietnamese macroeconomic evidence for 2000–2024, this study explores alternative investment scenarios. The simulations suggest that sustained investment can raise output and aggregate welfare, with gains depending on institutional capacity to convert public spending into productive knowledge. For policymakers, the implications are to strengthen project selection, accountable implementation, data governance and workforce skills alongside investment, and to phase expenditure according to implementation capacity. Reskilling and support for affected workers matter because aggregate gains do not ensure equal benefits across groups. These are conditional simulations using calibrated AI and digital capital stocks, not forecasts or direct estimates of realised economic effects. The framework can inform policy appraisal and public debate on how technology investment and institutional reform can jointly support Vietnam’s long-term development.

title: Towards a green China: energy policy, technological innovation, and green investment as drivers of environmental sustainability
summary: China’s pursuit of environmental sustainability has become one of the defining policy experiments of the twenty-first century, combining an ambitious dual-carbon pledge with the world’s largest deployment of clean-energy technology and green capital. This review synthesizes recent scholarship to examine how three interlocking levers, energy and climate policy, technological innovation, and green investment, jointly shape China’s transition toward a lower-carbon and more resilient development path. Drawing on a structured reading of peer-reviewed research published predominantly between 2019 and 2025, the article develops an integrated framework in which policy sets direction and incentives, innovation lowers the cost and expands the frontier of abatement, and investment mobilizes the capital required to translate intent into installed capacity. The evidence indicates that target-based governance, embodied in successive Five-Year Plans and the 2030/2060 carbon commitments, has been reinforced by market-based instruments such as the national emissions trading system, and by an expanding architecture of green credit and green bonds. Technological progress in solar photovoltaics, wind power, batteries, and electric mobility has driven steep learning curves, allowing renewable additions to exceed fossil capacity additions by wide margins in recent years. Green finance is shown across numerous provincial and firm-level studies to reduce carbon-emission intensity, chiefly by catalyzing green technological innovation and by reallocating capital away from pollution-intensive activities. Nevertheless, persistent tensions remain, including coal lock-in, energy-security concerns, uneven regional capacity, intensity-based rather than absolute caps, data-quality risks, and the danger of greenwashing. The review argues that the effectiveness of any single lever is conditional on its coherence with the others, and that spatial spillovers and regional heterogeneity mediate outcomes in ways that generic national narratives obscure. Case evidence is integrated throughout to ground the analysis in concrete provincial, sectoral, and corporate experience. The article closes by identifying priorities for policy design and an agenda for future research on the policy–innovation–investment nexus.

title: Carbon Emission Reduction and Earnings Management: The Moderating Roles of Board Gender Diversity and Board Remuneration in South African Carbon-Intensive Firms
summary: Earnings management (EM) remains a significant concern in corporate financial re-porting, particularly among carbon-intensive companies facing increasing pressure to demonstrate environmental responsibility (ER) while maintaining financial reporting credibility. This study investigates the moderating role of board gender diversity (BGD) and board remuneration (BR) on carbon emission reduction (CER)- earnings manage-ment (EM) relationship among Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE)-listed car-bon-intensive companies. This study adopts a quantitative panel data approach, exam-ining 106 companies over the period 2015–2025. Fixed-effects model is employed to es-timate the main relationships, while two-step system generalised method of moments estimation for additional robustness testing. The findings reveal a statistically significant negative relationship between CER and EM, suggesting that stronger carbon emission reduction is associated with reduced earnings management. Furthermore, the findings indicate that BGD and BR shape the CER–EM relationship, highlighting the importance of corporate governance mechanisms in financial reporting behaviour. The study con-tributes to the sustainability reporting literature by showing the relevance of board composition and remuneration arrangements in understanding the environmental re-sponsibility-financial reporting quality nexus.

title: Corporate Governance and Performance of Firm: Evidence from Firms Listed at the Nairobi Securities Exchange, Kenya
summary: The performance of firms listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE) remains important to economic growth, investor confidence, and capital market stability. However, empirical findings on the relationship between corporate governance and firm performance remain inconclusive. This study examined the effect of corporate governance on the performance of firms listed on the NSE. Guided by a positivist research philosophy and descriptive-correlational research design, the study analysed panel secondary data from 63 firms with complete data covering 2014-2025, obtained from published annual reports and reputable financial databases. Firm performance was measured using Tobin’s Q, while corporate governance was assessed using board size and board independence. Firm size, financial leverage, and firm age were included as control variables. Panel regression techniques, including pooled ordinary least squares, random effects, and fixed-effects models, were estimated, with the Hausman specification test guiding model selection. The findings revealed that corporate governance had a positive and statistically significant effect on firm performance. The study recommends that listed firms strengthen corporate governance mechanisms to enhance performance, while policymakers and regulators promote effective oversight and accountability. The study contributes empirical evidence to the corporate governance and firm performance literature in the context of the Kenyan capital market. Keywords: Corporate Governance, Firm Performance, Board Size, Board Independence, Tobin’s Q, Nairobi Securities Exchange.

title: A Multi-Level Perspective on Social Responsibility: From Corporate Practices to Individual Action in Sustainability
summary: Ethical behavior and sustainable development have increased interest in individual and social responsibility beyond corporate social responsibility. Individual Social Responsibility remains underexplored, with limited empirically validated measures. This study conceptualizes ISR and develops a multidimensional scale to assess individual responsibility toward social, public, and environmental issues followed by stakeholder theory. A mixed-method research design was employed. Measurement items were generated through a comprehensive review of CSR and sustainability literature and semi-structured interviews with CSR professionals and academics. Data were then collected from managerial and non-managerial employees in manufacturing and service-sector organizations of China. The proposed scale was evaluated using exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, reliability, convergent and discriminant validity, and unidimensionality tests. Results demonstrate that the ISR scale satisfies established statistical criteria and comprises three dimensions: social responsibility, public responsibility, and environmental responsibility. This study provides an empirically validated foundation for measuring ISR and organizations seeking to promote responsible individual behavior and sustainable societal development.

title: Audit Quality, the Fraud Diamond, and Fraudulent Financial Reporting: The Moderating Role of the Audit Committee in Indonesia's Consumer Sector
summary: Background: Fraudulent financial reporting is relatively infrequent but disproportionately costly, and recent fraud evidence continues to show the importance of detecting material misstatement risk (Association of Certified Fraud Examiners). Indonesian consumer cyclicals and non-cyclicals are analytically relevant because intense competition, performance targets, macroeconomic exposure, and long distribution chains can increase reporting pressure. Objective: This study tests the effects of audit quality and the fraud diamond on fraudulent financial reporting risk and examines audit committee activity as a moderator. Methods: The sampling frame comprised Indonesia Stock Exchange firms classified as consumer cyclicals or consumer non-cyclicals during 2020–2024. Purposive screening produced 100 eligible firms and 500 balanced firm-year observations. Panel regression selected the Common Effect Model, followed by mean-centered moderated regression and diagnostic tests. Results: Audit quality is negatively associated with fraudulent financial reporting risk, whereas financial target and external pressure are positively associated with it. The other fraud-diamond proxies are not significant. Audit committee activity strengthens the protective association of audit quality and weakens the positive association of financial target but does not moderate the remaining relationships. Conclusion: Pressure-related factors are the dominant significant fraud-diamond signals in this sample, while the audit committee operates as a selective complement to external audit rather than a universal safeguard.

title: The sectoral blind spot of green bonds in the European green transition
summary: Abstract As sustainable finance becomes the central engine of the European green transition, how green-bond proceeds map onto distinct environmental objectives remains poorly understood. This study provides cross-sectional econometric evidence on the macro-financial and environmental correlates of green-bond issuance across the EU-27. Defining market penetration as the green-bond share of total national corporate and sovereign issuance, we use four-year averages (2021–2024) to combine bivariate correlation with ordinary least squares regression. We find that issuance is associated with the share of renewable energy and environmental health but shows no detectable association with circular material use, ecosystem vitality, environmental taxation, or climate-change performance (R² = 0.44; renewable energy, p = 0.002; GDP per capita, p = 0.019; climate performance, p = 0.50). A concentration analysis further shows that participation broadened until 2021 and narrowed again in 2024 (Gini 0.85 in 2014, 0.48 in 2021, 0.79 in 2024) rather than rising steadily. These findings point to a critical policy challenge, as capital appears to follow institutional capacity and structural measurability rather than holistic climate ambition, creating a sectoral blind spot. To broaden the environmental reach of green bonds, we identify the standardisation of metrics for underfunded sectors – through the EU Taxonomy and the European Green Bond Standard – as the most direct policy lever.

title: Corporate Social Responsibility and Performance of Manufacturing Companies in Nigeria: A Literature Review
summary: The purpose of the study was to examine corporate social responsibility and performance of manufacturing companies in Nigeria. Corporate social responsibility of the business is composed of different components that are combined to form one whole concept. The pyramid of corporate social responsibility (CSR) describes the four different components that are unified with each other and provide framework how a business organization might engage in business decisions, actions, practices, and policies simultaneously. The study recommended that management of companies should often involve community stakeholders in CSR decision making in order to ensure a positive perception of the firms CSR performance by the host community.

title: Navigating boundary-less work: how family-supportive leadership reshapes the impact of work-family blurring on professional women’s job engagement and taking charge in the digital transformation
summary: In the context of a digital transformation that is fundamentally refining the nature of work and leadership dynamics, this research examines the mediating role of job engagement and the moderating role of family supportive supervisor behavior in the relationship between work-family role blurring and taking charge. A moderated mediation model is constructed using boundary theory and work-family border theory as foundational frameworks. The data were collected from 275 professional women in China. Moreover, family supportive supervisor behavior which is a key manifestation of supportive leadership in the modern, boundary-less workplace moderates the relationship between work-family role blurring and job engagement. Additionally, moderated mediation results confirm that a higher level of family supportive supervisor behavior increases professional women’s taking charge level through the indirect effect of work-family role blurring via job engagement. The findings highlight that in an era of pervasive digital connectivity, cultivating family supportive supervisor behaviors is a crucial strategy for management to mitigate role blurring and enhance professional women’s proactive workplace behaviors. This study enriches our understanding of the underlying processes of taking charge by developing a more comprehensive model that integrates the challenges of digital-era work design with the resource-providing function of leadership.

title: Strategic integration of business intelligence tools to enhance business management efficiency
summary: Purpose This study examines how data and business intelligence (BI) systems support procurement decisions and strategic execution. It aims to improve the efficiency of business management. Design/methodology/approach A five-stage implementation framework is proposed for integrating BI into strategic business execution. The methodology includes technical validation and a case study that assesses the impact of digital transformation and BI adoption on tracking strategic execution and key performance indicators (KPIs). We frame BI adoption within the broader digital transformation (DT) agenda, aligning data, processes and governance to strategic objectives. Findings Research shows that aligning digital transformation initiatives with an organization’s specific operational needs is the most cost-effective path to achieving efficiency. Analysis suggests that a successful digital transformation must be closely linked to the management requirements. Selecting appropriate BI tools is critical to delivering substantial business value. Research limitations/implications The proposed framework offers managers a structured approach to implementing BI systems aligned with strategic goals. The case study provides actionable insights for professionals aiming to improve operational and management performance through data-driven strategies and digital transformation. Originality/value The research contributes to the literature on digital transformation by presenting a structured, stage-gated framework for integrating BI tools into strategic management. It offers practical guidance for organizations seeking to enhance performance through data-informed decision-making, differentiating itself through a detailed implementation model developed and illustrated in a procurement context.

title: Key Drivers of Growth in Promoting Economic Growth Amid the Middle-Income Trap Challenges in ASEAN
summary: This study examines the effects of trade openness, interest rates, exchange rates, fiscal policy, the digital economy, and political stability on economic growth in middle-income ASEAN countries amid the challenges of the middle-income trap. Using a quantitative explanatory design, the study analyzes panel data from Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand over the 2014–2023 period. Secondary data were obtained from the World Development Indicators and Worldwide Governance Indicators and analyzed using panel data regression. The fixed effects model results show that trade openness has a positive and statistically significant effect on economic growth, whereas interest rates and fiscal policy have significant negative effects. Exchange rates, the digital economy, and political stability do not have statistically significant effects at the 5% significance level. Simultaneously, the six independent variables significantly explain variations in economic growth, with an adjusted coefficient of determination of 0.6753. These findings highlight the importance of international trade integration, manageable financing costs, and effective government expenditure in supporting economic growth. Addressing the middle-income trap requires not only expanding economic activity but also improving productivity, resource allocation, and the effectiveness of growth-enhancing policies.

title: Islamic corporate social responsibility as a governance-embedded system: evidence from Islamic banks in Malaysia and Indonesia
summary: Purpose Although there has been a rapid rate of expansion observed in the domain of Islamic banking, there remains an inconsistent degree of institutionalisation of Islamic corporate social responsibility (ICSR). The reason is that a higher priority level has been placed on contractual and financial compliance by existing CSR and Shariah governance models, rather than broader socio-economic aspects. The purpose of this study was to develop an ICSR framework to assess the capacity of existing Islamic banking institutions to institutionalise ICSR through relevant governance mechanisms and Islamic social finance instruments, while examining their relationships with socio-economic outcomes. Design/methodology/approach In this investigation, a qualitative multiple-case study design, which involved both Maybank Islamic (Malaysia) and Bank Syariah Indonesia (Indonesia), was employed. Specifically, semi-structured interviews were conducted with a total of 20 purposively selected senior informants, with 10 from each of the two institutions, who were directly involved in the process of ICSR governance and implementation. The interviews, which ranged between 60 and 120 min, were triangulated with corresponding institutional and sustainability documents. After collecting the data, a thematic content analysis was performed through the NVivo software, which incorporated iterative coding, intercoder verification, participant validation and cross-case comparison to identify relevant patterns of ICSR institutionalisation and socio-economic value creation. Findings The findings revealed a clear hierarchy of ICSR institutionalisation, wherein zakat represented the most formally embedded instrument, supported by Shariah oversight, structured procedures, auditing and reporting. Meanwhile, voluntary instruments, including sadaqah and infaq, and developmental instruments, such as qard al-hasan and waqf, exhibited weaker and more fragmented degrees of organisational integration. Four differentiated socio-economic outcome clusters were associated with the above instruments, namely, immediate relief and redistribution (zakat), community trust and relational legitimacy (sadaqah or infaq), economic empowerment (qard al-hasan) and long-term or intergenerational welfare (waqf). Importantly, the interview results demonstrated an institutionalisation–impact paradox, in which instruments associated with greater long-term developmental potential were not equivalent to those most strongly embedded within existing structures of governance. Practical implications A policy-relevant framework was provided for existing Islamic banking institutions, regulators and Shariah boards to strengthen the governance, coordination, measurement and reporting aspects of relevant ICSR instruments that were often under-institutionalised. The proposed framework could also inform the development of Shariah-specific social responsibility indicators that were aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), which could enable more substantive and comparable assessment of ICSR beyond conventional CSR reporting processes. Originality/value Islamic ethical underpinnings, Shariah governance structures, Islamic social finance tools and various socio-economic outcomes were incorporated in this study into a consolidated and empirically grounded framework. Particularly, it was demonstrated that there were varying levels of institutionalisation and socio-economic value observed in existing ICSR instruments, which highlighted the existence of an institutionalisation–impact paradox. As such, there was a deeper understanding of how Islamic obligations are converted from religious teachings into actual organisational practice and developmental value.

title: Implementasi Asas Otonomi Daerah Berdasarkan Undang-Undang Nomor 23 Tahun 2014 dalam Penanganan Kebakaran Hutan dan Lahan
summary: Forest and land fires (karhutla) remain a major environmental challenge in Indonesia. This study analyzes the implementation of the regional autonomy principle under Law Number 23 of 2014 on Regional Government in addressing forest and land fires, identifies the challenges faced by local governments, and assesses the effectiveness of regional autonomy in improving coordination, prevention, and mitigation. The research employs a normative juridical approach through library research on legislation, scientific literature, and official government data. The findings indicate that regional autonomy has enabled local governments to establish policies and institutions supporting fire management, including Regional Disaster Management Agencies (BPBD), Fire Control Task Forces, and community-based prevention programs. However, implementation faces obstacles such as limited budgets, human resources, and facilities, weak inter-agency coordination, and low public participation. Regional autonomy has improved coordination and emergency response, yet remains suboptimal due to continued dependence on central government support in technology, funding, and law enforcement. Therefore, strengthening local institutional capacity, cross-sectoral coordination, and community participation is essential for more effective and sustainable environmental governance.

title: ENVIRONMENTAL PERFORMANCE, SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY, AND FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE OF INDONESIAN BANKS: THE MODERATING ROLE OF GOOD CORPORATE GOVERNANCE
summary: This study examines the relationships of environmental performance and social responsibility with financial performance and tests good corporate governance as a moderator in Indonesian banking. A quantitative associative design uses annual and sustainability reports for 15 purposively selected banks during 2020–2024, yielding 75 bank-year observations. Environmental performance is measured using the Green Banking Disclosure Index, social responsibility using the Corporate Social Responsibility Disclosure Index, and financial performance using return on assets. Governance is represented by a reverse-coded self-assessment score. The analysis uses multiple linear regression and moderated regression analysis in IBM SPSS 25. Its reported analysis identifies positive, statistically significant direct relationships for environmental performance and social responsibility, with an R² of 0.301 and an adjusted R² of 0.281. The environmental performance–governance interaction is not significant (p = .419), nor is the social responsibility–governance interaction (p = .789). These reported findings suggest that sustainability disclosure and governance should be assessed as distinct dimensions of bank management. However, inconsistencies within the reported regression diagnostics and coefficient tables require verification. The evidence should therefore be interpreted as provisional, sample-specific associations rather than causal effects or proof that governance has no moderating role.

title: Sustainable Finance in Nigeria: Overview, Enablers, Benefits and Challenges
summary: ABSTRACT: Sustainable finance is a key tool to link financial decision-making with environmental integrity, social inclusion and long term economic resilience. Its agenda is consequential for Nigeria: the country's challenge is to increase energy access, infrastructure, employment, productive investment, accommodate vulnerability to climate change, curtail pollution, biodiversity loss and the risks of a gradual global shift from high-carbon activity. This conceptual review analyzes sustainable finance in Nigeria using Nigerian policy and market documents, and selected international research and standards. It defines the concept and scope of sustainable finance; outlines key instruments and institutional enablers of sustainable finance; evaluates the environmental, economic, social and financial-stability benefits of sustainable finance; and explores potential barriers to ensuring capital flows into sustainable finance that impact its ability to generate tangible development results. The review views Nigeria's sovereign green-bond issuance and its Sustainable Bond Framework as a measure of institutional development but not as an indicator of the current state of the green-bond marketplace or a guarantee of a sustainable financed outcome. The analysis pinpoints recurring difficulties related to long-term capital, the availability of currency and macroeconomic risk, hurdles in project preparation, the lack of reliable sustainability information, skills deficits, scattered coordination and poor monitoring as well as the potential of "green washing. Suggests a context specific approach based on five elements: policy credibility, project pipelines that can be invested, financial intermediation, disclosure and verification, inclusion, and outcome measurement. The main thrust is not only the amount of labelled instruments, but also the additionality, integrity, affordability and distributional equity of sustainable finance and iAl-Amin (2025) independently demonstrated environmental and social outcomes in Nigeria. The article ends with policy priorities and a research agenda to further build a more credible, inclusive and developmentally robust sustainable finance ecosystem. title: Ecology and Sustainability in the 21st Century: An Interdisciplinary Integrative and Critical Review with a Focus on Portugal
summary: Sustainability is an interdisciplinary scientific and institutional challenge that isolated improvements in technological efficiency, emissions reduction, or material substitution cannot adequately address. This study presents an interdisciplinary, integrative, and critical review of ecology and sustainability, complemented by documentary analysis and selected case studies. It examines ecological integrity, biodiversity, biophysical constraints, economic systems, environmental governance, and the distribution of environmental impacts across territories and generations, with particular attention to Portugal. The analysis highlights the limitations of treating efficiency, circularity, and innovation as sufficient evidence of environmental sustainability. Robust assessment requires explicit system boundaries, comparable functional units, consideration of indirect effects, and attention to the displacement of environmental costs. Selected SCI research cases illustrate the importance of evidence traceability and the limits of quantitative conclusions when underlying data cannot be adequately reconciled. The study distinguishes established scientific knowledge, documented SCI findings, and analytical interpretations. It does not constitute a systematic review or a scoping review conducted under PRISMA-ScR. Its conclusions are limited to the evidence examined. The paper contributes an interdisciplinary framework for understanding sustainability as preserving ecological functions alongside human well-being, social justice, and long-term institutional responsibility.

title: From E-Government to Algorithmic Governance
summary: Digital governance and digital-era governance mark a major paradigm shift in how the state and local administration function, driven by the growing role of digital technologies in government organization, state operations, and state-citizen relations. Although the literature has addressed e-government, digital transformation, and technology-enabled public management comprehensively, gaps remain in conceptual foundations, theoretical synthesis, and methodological approaches. This paper presents a bibliometric and science-mapping overview of digital governance studies from 2011 to 2025 to identify the field's intellectual development, collaborative structure, topical directions, and emerging research areas. By doing so, the study aims to move beyond descriptive evaluations and provide a theoretically informed account of governance transformation in the digital and algorithmic age.

title: Does the carbon emission trading scheme enhance enterprises’ green total factor productivity? Evidence from China
summary: With growing global attention to climate change and sustainable development, the green and low-carbon transition has become a key pathway to advancing high-quality economic development. However, whether the carbon emission trading scheme can enhance enterprises’ green total factor productivity while simultaneously achieving emission reductions still requires further investigation. Utilizing relevant data of Chinese A-share listed companies spanning from 2011 to 2023, the present study conceptualizes the carbon emission trading scheme as a quasi-natural experiment and establishes a Difference-in-Differences (DID) model to scrutinize its impact on enterprises’ green total factor productivity (GTFP). The findings reveal that the carbon emission trading scheme notably elevates enterprises’ GTFP, with the outcomes retaining robustness even after addressing endogeneity concerns and conducting rigorous robustness checks. Mechanism tests elucidate that the carbon emission trading scheme primarily propels enterprises’ GTFP by alleviating financing constraints, curtailing agency costs, and promoting digital transformation. Moderating effect tests demonstrate that market competition plays a pivotal role in amplifying the positive influence of the carbon emission trading scheme on enterprises’ GTFP. Heterogeneity analysis suggests that the policy effects of the trading scheme are more noticeable among non-state-owned enterprises, pollution-intensive enterprises, and enterprises situated in the eastern region. Furthermore, an examination of economic consequences unveils that the carbon emission trading scheme not only elevates their GTFP but also fosters their high-quality development. These research outcomes not only diversify the theoretical literature concerning the trading scheme and its economic consequences but also furnish vital theoretical guidance and policy recommendations for refining the carbon emission trading scheme, advancing the construction of the trading market, and bolstering enterprises’ GTFP.

title: Governance Configurations and Corporate Green Innovation: A Configurational Analysis
summary: ABSTRACT Green innovation has become a strategic choice for firms responding to environmental regulation and seeking competitive advantage. Prior research has focused primarily on the independent effects of internal and external governance elements, yet how these elements combine into configurations remains underexplored. Drawing on stakeholder theory, this study adopts a configurational perspective and employs fuzzy‐set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to examine how internal and external governance elements jointly shape green innovation. The findings reveal three pathways: externally‐driven, internally‐driven, and synergistic balanced. No single governance element is necessary for high green innovation. The relationship among external governance elements depends on internal governance strength. When internal governance is limited, government subsidies, green investors, and supply chain finance operate synergistically. When internal governance is strong, government support and market capital become substitutable. The relationship among internal governance elements depends on the dominant resource source. When internal resources dominate, shareholder balance, executive compensation intensity, and technical directors reinforce one another. When external resources dominate, technical directors and executive compensation intensity appear in mutually exclusive configurations. These findings suggest that effective governance depends on coherence among selected elements rather than comprehensiveness across all dimensions. The study extends the stakeholder theory tradition on prioritization and trade‐offs by identifying the configurational conditions under which governance elements operate in synergy, substitution, or mutual exclusivity, offering a configurational lens for understanding corporate green innovation governance.

title: From Green Digital Transformation to Hotel Performance: The Roles of Dynamic Capabilities, Innovation Capabilities, and Organizational Resilience
summary: The hotel industry has acknowledged the growing environmental concern and recognized the significance of adopting sustainable practices. The existing literature on the hotel industry reflects a discernible gap between green digital transformation and green dynamic capabilities, green innovation capabilities, and organizational resilience. Therefore, this study aims to examine the relationships between green digital transformation, green dynamic capabilities, green innovation capabilities, organizational resilience, and organizational performance. Using purposive sampling, data were gathered from 329 managers working in four Chinese cities and analyzed through partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings highlight the significant positive association between green digital transformation, green dynamic capabilities and green innovation capabilities, which, in turn, are positively associated with hotel resilience. Furthermore, organizational resilience is significantly associated with process innovation, service innovation, and organizational performance. Practically, the study’s findings help encourage hotel managers to implement digital technologies to improve hotels’ efficiency and organizational performance. Moreover, the study encourages regulatory authorities to support green digitalization initiatives and improve hotels’ performances.

title: Strategic Communication and Corporate Reputation Management: An Evaluation of Select Blue-Chip Firms in Rivers State, Nigeria
summary: This study examined the strategic communication approaches adopted by select blue-chip firms in Rivers State, Nigeria, and their effectiveness in managing corporate reputation. Anchored on the Excellence Theory and the Situational Crisis Communication Theory (SCCT), the study explored how TotalEnergies and Nigeria Liquefied Natural Gas (NLNG) utilise corporate social responsibility (CSR), stakeholder engagement, crisis communication, and digital media to strengthen stakeholder trust and enhance reputational capital. A descriptive survey research design was adopted, and data were collected from 360 respondents drawn from both organisations using the Krejcie and Morgan (1970) sample size determination table. The instrument, a structured questionnaire, was validated by experts and achieved a reliability coefficient above 0.80 using Cronbach’s Alpha. Data were analysed using frequencies, weighted means, and percentages. Findings revealed that CSR and stakeholder engagement significantly enhance organisational credibility and public trust, while crisis communication practices were often constrained by bureaucratic delay and limited digital responsiveness. The study confirms that an integrated communication approach improves transparency, legitimacy, and long-term corporate sustainability. Theoretically, it extends the Excellence Theory and SCCT within an African context, emphasising the influence of socio-political and infrastructural factors on communication effectiveness. The study recommends a proactive communication framework combining CSR, stakeholder inclusion, and transparent digital interaction to sustain corporate reputation in complex business environments.

title: Corporate reputation in India: unveiling the role of board dimensions
summary: Purpose The primary motive of this research is to quantify corporate reputation by developing a reputation index along with investigating the influence of governance mechanisms, specifically board characteristics, on the reputation of Indian firms. Design/methodology/approach Reputation of 249 manufacturing firms listed in the National Stock Exchange (NSE) 500 index has been analysed over the period 2015–2024 using a reputation index, and to further investigate its association with board dynamics, panel data analysis has been employed. Findings Results reveal that board dimensions at firms in India have a huge contribution in impacting their reputation. Specifically, larger boards negatively affect corporate reputation, adding credence to agency theory, while board independence enhances it. Research limitations/implications This study enriches the corporate governance literature by empirically linking board attributes with corporate reputation in the Indian context. Practical implications The findings suggest that firms should prioritise the appointment of independent directors while maintaining optimal board size to improve their reputational standing. Furthermore, the reputation index developed in this study offers investors an additional tool to evaluate potential investments by providing firms' reputation scores. Social implications The article contains valuable insights for shareholders who must be aware of how effective governance mechanisms help to build corporate reputation. Originality/value The present study is novel in examining the association between board dynamics and corporate reputation in India in the post-Companies Act, 2013 context. It further develops a reputation index using several proxies for measuring firms' reputation quantitatively, offering a distinctive contribution to the literature.

title: ADOPTION OF INTERNATIONAL FINANCIAL REPORTING STANDARD AND VALUE RELEVANCE OF ACCOUNTING INFORMATION IN NIGERIA
summary: This study examined the adoption of international financial reporting standard and value relevance of accounting information in Nigeria. The specific objectives were to determine the effect of PRE-IFRS adoption on the earnings per share of selected companies in Nigeria and to ascertain the effect of POST-IFRS adoption on the earnings per share of selected companies in Nigeria. The study adopted an ex-post facto research design. The population with consists of all listed companies in Nigeria. The sample size for the study consisted of Dangote Sugar Plc, Cussons Nigeria Plc, Nigeria Breweries Plc, and Nestle Nigeria Plc. Data were sourced from the financial statements of Dangote Sugar Plc, Cussons Nigeria Plc, Nigeria Breweries Plc, and Nestle Nigeria Plc. The study was analyzed using panel regression. The findings of this study revealed that PRE-IFRS adoption has a positive and insignificant effect on the earnings per share of selected companies in Nigeria, whereas POST-IFRS adoption has a positive and insignificant effect on the earnings per share of selected companies in Nigeria. In conclusion, the adoption of IFRS tends to enhance the value relevance of accounting information, but its success depends on contextual factors and the commitment of all stakeholders involved in the financial reporting ecosystem of a particular company. The study recommended that companies should ensure that a timely and full implementation of IFRS is implemented to encourage and unlock the actual financial performance benefits accompanied by adopting IFRS in the country.

title: Good Governance Mechanisms and Corporate Social Responsibility Integration: A Scoping Review of Frameworks, Practices, and Gaps in Philippine Business Entities
summary: Abstract Over the past decade, how Philippine businesses balance accountability, profit, and social impact has shifted dramatically from voluntary charitable giving to formal requirements that tie environmental and social commitments directly to core governance structures. This scoping review systematically maps what we know about this integration, what evidence exists, and what critical questions remain unanswered for Philippine business entities between January 2016 and June 2026. Following the widely accepted scoping review structure from Arksey and O’Malley (2005) and PRISMA-ScR reporting rules from Tricco et al. (2018), the study draws on 62 credible sources: peer-reviewed research, government regulatory orders, multilateral agency reports, and industry practice guidelines. The analysis shows that while recent policies including SEC Memorandum Circular No. 16-2025 now make sustainability disclosure mandatory for many firms, meaningful progress is uneven. Publicly listed companies and state-owned enterprises have moved fastest to align governance and responsibility, but private firms, family-run businesses, and the micro, small, and medium enterprise (MSME) sector 99.6% of all registered Philippine businesses struggle to embed these practices into daily operations. Stronger integration links directly to independent board oversight, dedicated sustainability committees, and genuine engagement with workers and communities, while persistent barriers include limited resources, vague rules for non-listed firms, and global standards that do not fit local realities. This review fills key gaps in cross-sector research and offers actionable direction for policy, business practice, and doctoral-level inquiry especially for understanding how governance and responsibility shape operational resilience and productivity, core concerns in Advanced Production and Operations Management.

title: The impact of the digital economy on agricultural green development and spatial spillover effects
summary: The transition toward greener agricultural production increasingly depends on the effective integration of digital technologies into rural production and service systems. Using a balanced panel covering 30 provincial-level regions in China from 2013 to 2024, this study evaluates the relationship between digital-economy development and agricultural green development (AGD). The two multidimensional indices are calculated through the entropy-weighting method. The empirical analysis proceeds through province and year fixed effects, a mediation framework, threshold estimation, and a spatial Durbin specification. The results show that higher digital-economy development is associated with a significant improvement in AGD. Agricultural technology innovation constitutes a transmission channel and accounts for 12.67% of the estimated effect. The relationship is also conditional on rural human capital: after rural human capital crosses the estimated threshold, the positive association becomes noticeably stronger. Regional estimates reveal substantial heterogeneity, with the eastern provinces exhibiting a larger effect than the central and western regions. Spatial decomposition further indicates that the influence of digital development extends beyond provincial boundaries, and the estimated spillover effect is greater than the within-province direct effect. Taken together, the findings suggest that digital transformation in agriculture depends not only on technological infrastructure but also on local absorptive capacity and cross-regional linkages. The results therefore highlight the importance of strengthening rural human capital, agricultural technology diffusion, and interregional cooperation in the process of agricultural green transformation.

title: The Impact of Digital Economy and Industrial Agglomeration on Green Total Factor Productivity: An Analysis of Mechanisms and Regulatory Conditions
summary: This paper examines the relationship between digital economy development, manufacturing agglomeration, and urban green total factor productivity (GTFP). Using an unbalanced panel of 283 Chinese prefecture-level cities over 2007–2022, we estimate a two-way fixed-effects model that includes digital development, manufacturing agglomeration, and their interaction. The interaction coefficient is positive and statistically significant, indicating that the association between manufacturing agglomeration and GTFP becomes more favorable as digital development increases. Sequential regressions link this relationship to lower capital misallocation, better labor allocation, and greater green patent activity, with stronger statistical support for the green-innovation channel. The lagged specification and environmental-performance outcome provide further supporting evidence. Subsample estimates provide suggestive evidence of a larger interaction coefficient in cities with higher environmental-regulation intensity. These findings connect digital development and manufacturing concentration with urban green productivity and highlight the relevance of factor allocation, green innovation, and regulatory conditions to the green transformation of industrial clusters.

title: Integrating Customer Profitability Analysis into Retail Banking Strategic Planning: A Case Study of Bank Syariah Indonesia in Makassar
summary: Digital transformation has increased the strategic relevance of customer-level financial information in retail banking, although its managerial application within Islamic banking remains insufficiently understood. This study examined how Customer Profitability Analysis (CPA) was interpreted and incorporated into strategic planning at Bank Syariah Indonesia, Makassar Area. A qualitative case study employed an in-depth, semi-structured interview with the Retail and Transaction Business Manager, supported by corporate reports and institutional documents. Thematic analysis identified three interrelated dimensions: the construction of customer profitability, its application to relationship management, and adaptation to local and Sharia-related considerations. Profitability assessments encompassed account balances, fee-based income, digital transactions, financing characteristics, collectibility risks, and service costs. These considerations informed customer segmentation, differentiated services, retention, cross-selling, up-selling, and marketing resource allocation. Managerial interpretations also reflected local interest in gold-related banking products and the financing needs of micro, small, and medium enterprises, alongside principles of justice and public benefit. CPA consequently functioned as a context-sensitive decision-support framework rather than a verified calculation of customer-level net profitability. Evidence from one managerial informant and secondary documents limits transferability and prevents claims of measured financial improvement. The findings clarify how accounting information can inform strategic choices while accommodating financial inclusion objectives within local markets.

title: Mechanisms Through Which Supply Chain Vertical Integration Improves Corporate Debt Financing Costs: A Multi-Case Study of BYD, NIO and XPeng
summary: Against the backdrop of volatile global raw material prices and supply chain restructuring, the new energy vehicle (NEV) industry exhibits two coexisting modes of supply chain organization, namely vertical integration on the one hand and external procurement or contract manufacturing on the other. Taking BYD as the focal case and NIO and XPeng as comparative cases, and drawing on the three companies’ public annual reports, bond offering circulars, credit rating reports and ESG reports for 2020 to 2025, this paper investigates through which channels supply chain vertical integration affects corporate debt financing costs. The analysis proceeds along the transaction cost line and the information disclosure line, and examines under what conditions digitalization, institutional complexity and ESG performance strengthen or weaken this process. The findings are interpreted on the basis of transaction cost theory and information asymmetry theory, and the divergence in measurement arising from accounting-based indicators of debt cost is clarified.

title: Do the Corporate Governance Framework Mechanism Affect Sustainability Reporting in Food Beverage Companies?
summary: This study aims to examine the influence of corporate governance mechanisms on sustainability reporting within food and beverage (F&B) companies listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange for the 2021–2024 period. The research is motivated by increasing stakeholder demands for transparency regarding environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosures, as well as the significance of sustainability reporting as a form of legitimacy for a company’s internal responsibilities—reflected in its business strategy and long-term sustainability. The study utilizes secondary data obtained from companies' financial and sustainability reports. Panel data regression analysis is employed to test the impact of the independent variables—specifically corporate governance mechanisms, comprising board size, the presence of female directors, independent directors, and foreign directors—on sustainability reporting. The findings indicate that corporate governance mechanisms do not influence the level of sustainability reporting. None of the governance variables were found to have a significant effect on promoting sustainability reporting within these companies. Consequently, the implementation of corporate governance roles, particularly within the F&B sector, has yet to effectively enhance sustainability reporting. Keywords: sustainability reporting; female, independent and foreign directors; ESC.

title: The mediating role of trust: how CSR practices influence the behavioral intentions of hotel guests in Egypt’s Red Sea
summary: Purpose This study aims to investigate the mechanisms through which hotels’ corporate social responsibility (CSR) practices influence guest behavioral intentions, with a specific focus on the mediating role of trust within the distinctive setting of Egypt’s Red Sea region. Design/methodology/approach Adopting a quantitative methodology, a structured questionnaire was developed based on established CSR dimensions in the hospitality literature. Data were collected through an online survey from 399 visitors to Red Sea hotels in Egypt. Hypotheses were tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), with all three CSR dimensions entered simultaneously into a unified model and key demographic variables included as control variables. Findings Using PLS-SEM with all CSR dimensions estimated simultaneously, trust fully mediates the relationships between guest CSR and both revisit and word-of-mouth intentions, and partially mediates environmental CSR’s effect on revisit intentions. Social CSR changed sign when the other dimensions were controlled, a pattern for which competing explanations are examined rather than asserted. Trust does not carry CSR into spending intentions as it carries loyalty and advocacy: the mediated pathway to spending is negative for environmental and guest CSR, and the small positive value for social CSR is the arithmetic product of two negative coefficients rather than a trust-based route to expenditure. This reveals a broad disconnect between trust-building CSR and financial commitment. Originality/value This research addresses a significant gap by deconstructing CSR into specific practices and examining their distinct effects on different behavioral outcomes through the lens of trust. The findings provide insights for managers in developing economies, suggesting that while CSR builds trust and influences loyalty and advocacy, it may not be sufficient to directly command the spending intentions of the guests.

title: Integrating digital financial solutions into MSME business models: assessment of MSME readiness for digital financial integration
summary: The integration of digital financial solutions has become essential for enhancing the sustainability and competitiveness of Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), especially in developing economies. This study examined MSME readiness in terms of digital capability, financial literacy, infrastructure readiness, and strategic orientation in relation to the integration of digital financial systems. Using a quantitative, cross-sectional research design, data were collected from 189 MSMEs in Surigao del Sur, Philippines, and analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation, and regression techniques. The findings revealed a strong positive relationship between MSME readiness and the level of digital financial integration. MSMEs with higher levels of readiness demonstrated greater improvements in business performance, operational efficiency, and financial stability, whereas those with lower levels of readiness gained only limited benefits. The results also indicated that full and systematic integration produced better outcomes than partial adoption. Overall, the study highlights that readiness is a key driver of successful digital transformation among MSMEs and emphasizes the need for targeted interventions to strengthen their capabilities and support sustainable digital finance adoption.

title: Analysis of ZARA's Supply Chain and Its Implications for China's Fast Fashion Industry
summary: In the digital economy era, apparel fashion trends evolve rapidly amid growing uncertainty in market demand. China's fast fashion industry faces challenges including fiercer market competition and climbing overall costs. As a leading brand in the fast fashion sector, ZARA still offers valuable insights with its distinctive supply chain management model, despite its continuous contraction in the Chinese market. Adopting a case study approach and based on the theories of supply chain rapid response mechanisms, inventory coordination, and flexible production, this paper draws on both domestic and international literature to conduct an in-depth analysis of ZARA's supply chain model as a representative case. This article analyzes ZARA's operational model from four dimensions: design, production, logistics, and inventory. It summarizes the company's strengths and current shortcomings and explores the implications for China's fast-fashion apparel industry. The results show that ZARA's agile fast response supply chain management model enables rapid responses to market demand, but it also faces issues such as high investment costs, inadequate product quality control, and significant environmental pressures. Instead of copying ZARA's model outright, Chinese fast fashion firms should draw on ZARA's rapid response mechanism, demand-oriented flexible production, small-batch production model, and inventory collaboration practices, adapt them to their own circumstances, advance information collaboration and leverage digitalization to strengthen market adaptability for greater market competitiveness.

title: Resource-based competencies and digital maturity: a synergistic approach to enhancing SME operational efficiency in Sub-Saharan Africa
summary: Abstract Although digital maturity offers transformative potential for SMEs, many in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) fail to realise proportional efficiency gains due to weak internal competencies. This study examines how resource-based and dynamic capabilities interact with digital maturity to enhance operational efficiency. Guided by an integrative theoretical framework that combines the Resource-Based View (RBV), Dynamic Capabilities Theory (DCT), the Technology–Organisation–Environment (TOE) framework, and complementary behavioural and institutional perspectives, the study employs a predictive cross-sectional design using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). Data were collected from 9,826 SMEs across thirteen SSA countries. The findings reveal that digital maturity significantly improves operational efficiency, with innovation capability and strategic alignment as mediators. Agility and institutional pressure amplify the digital–efficiency relationship. The study offers a contextualised, empirically validated model for SME digital transformation in resource-constrained environments. Though internal competencies and top-management support do not significantly moderate the digital-performance nexus, agility and institutional pressures amplify the transformative impact of digital maturity. SME digital strategies should prioritise capability development alongside technology deployment. Policymakers should design supportive regulatory and capacity-building frameworks, while technology vendors and financial institutions align products with firms’ absorptive capacities and agility levels. This study offers a novel, empirically validated model of SME digital transformation tailored to low-resource, high-uncertainty environments. By conceptualising digital maturity as a dynamic, capability-driven process, it advances theory and provides actionable insights for strategic capability building in digitally evolving SMEs. summary: The findingsof the study indicate that Azerbaijan has achieved significant progress in the key enabling factors of digitaldevelopment. These include high internet penetration, widespread mobile connectivity, and the rapid growth of cashlesspayment systems. However, the analysis also reveals that the large-scale adoption of advanced artificial intelligence andBig Data solutions remains limited, with many platforms relying on basic digital functionalities rather than fullyintegrated, intelligence-driven systems. title: Artificial Intelligence, Auditor Trust, and Fraud Detection in FinTech Audits: Evidence from Iraq
summary: FinTech has shifted financial activity towards platforms that generate high-volume, high-velocity transaction data, creating new opportunities for fraud. This study examines the association between AI-enabled auditing and auditors' perceived fraud-detection effectiveness in FinTech environments, and whether this association varies with auditors' trust in AI tools. Drawing on trust-in-automation and technology acceptance research, we surveyed 214 auditors engaged with Iraqi banks and licensed electronic payment providers and tested the hypotheses using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) with bootstrapped moderation analysis. The results show a positive association between AI-enabled auditing and perceived fraud-detection effectiveness. Auditor trust in AI has no statistically significant direct association with detection effectiveness, but it positively moderates the association between AI-enabled auditing and fraud detection: the estimated association is approximately 2.6 times stronger among high-trust auditors than among low-trust auditors. Trust therefore appears to act as a moderating condition rather than an independent predictor of perceived detection effectiveness. The study extends the discussion of audit technology beyond adoption to consider how trust conditions its perceived effectiveness. It also provides evidence from an emerging FinTech market in which research remains limited. For regulators, audit firms and FinTech supervisors, the findings suggest the importance of calibrated rather than uncritical trust in AI, supported by explainable tools, targeted training and clear guidance on AI-generated audit evidence.
