title: An Assessment of Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) Reporting Implementation in Public Sector Institutions. A Case Study of the University of Ghana
summary: Abstract This study assessed the implementation of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) reporting in public sector institutions, using the University of Ghana as a case study. Specifically, it examined the level of awareness and understanding of ESG reporting, current ESG related practices, implementation challenges, and opportunities for improving transparency and accountability. The study adopted a descriptive qualitative research design. Ten employees with relevant experience in administration, finance, planning, auditing, procurement, sustainability, governance, and quality assurance were purposively selected. Data was collected through semi structured interviews and analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings revealed varying levels of ESG awareness, with employees in strategic administrative and governance roles demonstrating greater understanding. Although the University undertakes several environmental, social, and governance activities, including waste management, energy conservation, student and staff welfare, community engagement, internal auditing, financial accountability, and procurement controls, these activities remain fragmented and are not integrated within a formal ESG reporting framework. Major challenges identified included the absence of an institutional ESG policy, limited expertise and resources, fragmented data systems, inconsistent reporting formats, weak coordination, and inadequate dedicated personnel. Nevertheless, ESG reporting was found to offer significant opportunities for strengthening transparency, accountability, stakeholder confidence, institutional reputation, evidence based decision making, resource allocation, and performance monitoring. The study concludes that effective ESG implementation requires a formal policy, standardized indicators, centralized coordination, staff capacity building, technological support, strong leadership commitment, and active stakeholder participation. These measures would consolidate existing initiatives into a credible, consistent, coordinated, institution wide ESG reporting system.

title: Digital Transformation Strategies for Sustainable Organizational and Workforce Development
summary: Digital transformation has become a highly useful approach that organizations can employ to increase operational efficiency, innovation, competitiveness, and sustainable development. The introduction of technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing, IoT, big data analytics, automation, and digital collaboration platforms affects the way in which organizations deliver value and manage their resources. Nonetheless, digital transformation entails more than the introduction of innovative technologies. The restructuring of organizations, training of their employees, development of their digital skills, leadership, culture, cybersecurity practices, and governance are all essential aspects of digital transformation. The paper focuses on the ways in which digital transformation strategies may lead to sustainable development of organizations by enhancing the capabilities of their employees. The study deals with the interrelationships between digital technologies, organizational operations, sustainability, employee capabilities, and strategic decision-making. Special emphasis is put on such aspects of digital transformation as digital skills development, reskilling and upskilling, digital leadership, data-driven decision-making, process optimization, employee engagement, and flexibility in work organization. Major barriers are also addressed. In addition, a theoretical framework is put forth which outlines how digital transformation could have an impact on economic, social, and environmental sustainability via organizational and workforce development approaches. Finally, it is concluded in the study that organizations can ensure sustainability in their digital transformations when technology adoption is combined with human-centered approaches to workforces.

title: Making agentic AI explainable and auditable
summary: Agentic AI promises operational speed, yet in finance, opaque decision paths hinder regulatory auditability. We address this autonomy paradox with a knowledge-enabled explainability (KEE) design theory that makes compliance an intrinsic, explicitly governed system property. KEE decouples probabilistic learning from an explicit, rule-governed reasoning layer, relocating epistemic uncertainty from opaque model inference to a semantic structure that can be inspected, contested, and updated. This enables ante-hoc structural control through a semantic, programmable graph that encodes regulatory mandates as executable, inspectable constraints. The theory specifies three design principles: structural knowledge codification, topological reasoning scaffolding, and adaptive synchronization. It also introduces six guidelines that operationalize regulator-acceptable, path-based audit trails. A longitudinal study of a multinational fintech platform provides naturalistic evidence that KEE can support high-velocity operations while producing path-based audit trails and accommodating controlled changes to regulatory logic. The study contributes to design science by theorizing auditable autonomy as ante-hoc structural control, specifying the entity-concept-event paradigm as its ontological mechanism, and formalizing this mechanism as a prescriptive design theory for regulated agentic AI.

title: ESG Credibility and Firm Profitability in An Emerging Market: Evidence from ESG Controversies and ESG Gap in Indonesia
summary: ESG is an important channel for a firm's relationship with its stakeholders. The firms are required to not only focus on profit, but they should also consider environmental, social, and governance. This study examines the relationship between Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) performance and firm profitability in an emerging market, with a particular emphasis on ESG credibility. Using a balanced panel dataset of 58 firms listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) over the period 2021–2024 (232 firm-year observations), this study employs ESG data from Refinitiv/LSEG and annual financial statements to measure profitability using Return on Assets (ROA). The empirical model is estimated using fixed-effects panel regression with firm-level clustered robust standard errors. The results indicate that the direct relationship between ESG performance and profitability is not supported in the Indonesian context. However, reputational risk plays a critical role: ESG controversies are significantly associated with profitability, and when operationalized as a high-controversy indicator (Controversy High), this variable exerts a negative effect on ROA. The key finding of this study demonstrates that the ESG Gap (ESG Score − ESGC) has a negative and highly significant impact on ROA, indicating the presence of a credibility penalty when the discrepancy between headline ESG performance and controversy-adjusted ESG scores widens. Robustness tests using an alternative profitability proxy (Net Margin) and alternative ESG measures confirm that the direct effect of ESG on profitability is relatively weak, whereas ESG credibility indicators are more informative. This study contributes to the literature by reinforcing the ESG credibility perspective and providing empirical evidence of reputational penalties and potential greenwashing in emerging markets. title: THEORETICAL AND METHODOLOGICAL FOUNDATIONS FOR DEVELOPING MANAGEMENT ACCOUNTING AS THE INFORMATION AND ANALYTICAL BASIS OF TAX MANAGEMENT FOR BUSINESS ENTITIES IN THE CONTEXT OF SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT
summary: The relevance of the study stems from increasing requirements for tax transparency, responsible business conduct, sound corporate governance, and timely responses to tax risks. Under these conditions, management accounting should provide internal users not only with data on revenues, costs, assets, liabilities, cash flows, and performance outcomes, but also with a relevant analytical basis for tax planning, tax-payment budgeting, control over the tax consequences of managerial alternatives, and monitoring of tax compliance. The purpose of the article is to develop theoretical and methodological provisions for integrating management accounting and tax management while considering the economic, social, and governance dimensions of sustainable development. The study applies a systems approach, methods of analysis and synthesis, comparison, generalization, structural and logical modelling, and a risk-oriented approach. It examines the functional interrelationship among management accounting, tax management, internal control, and ESG-oriented governance. The article proposes a model for building information and analytical support that encompasses the identification of tax-relevant transactions, collection and systematization of accounting data, assessment of tax consequences, risk ranking, selection of managerial alternatives, control over the fulfilment of tax obligations, and monitoring of the completeness of tax disclosures. A system of indicators is developed that includes the tax burden ratio, deviations of actual tax payments from the tax budget, an integrated tax-risk indicator, indicators of timeliness of settlements, tax losses, and tax-information transparency. The practical significance of the proposed provisions lies in their potential to improve the quality of managerial decision-making, proactively reduce tax risks, optimize cash flows, strengthen internal control, and enhance stakeholders’ trust in the tax conduct of business entities.

title: Digital transformation and circular economy practices in SMEs: Green transition and technological uncertainty
summary: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in emerging economies face increasing pressure to adopt circular economy practices, yet they often lack the resources to do so. This study examines whether, how, and under what technological conditions digital transformation enables such practices. Drawing on the dynamic capabilities view, we propose that digital transformation fosters a green transition, defined as the reorientation of technologies, routines, and commitments toward environmental sustainability, which in turn supports circular economy practices, and that technological uncertainty conditions these relationships. Survey data from 286 Vietnamese SMEs were analyzed with regression-based conditional process analysis, and the results were verified with partial least squares structural equation modeling. Three findings emerge. First, digital transformation is associated with circular economy practices both directly and indirectly through green transition, which accounts for approximately one-third of the total effect. Second, technological uncertainty weakens the relationship between digital transformation and green transition, indicating that digital resources are converted into greener operations less readily when technology changes rapidly. Third, technological uncertainty does not significantly alter the direct or the indirect effect of digital transformation on circular economy practices, which suggests that established green and circular routines are largely insulated from technological turbulence. The study clarifies the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which digitalization contributes to circularity and offers guidance to managers and policymakers on the sequencing of digital and green investments in SMEs.

title: Unveiling ESG ratings: corporate perspectives and institutionalisation dynamics
summary: Purpose Environmental, social and governance (ESG) ratings have become a central mechanism for assessing, benchmarking and signalling corporate sustainability performance to financial investors. Yet, their widespread use persists despite ongoing criticism of their capacity to accurately reflect firms’ social and environmental contributions. This paper aims to examine this paradox from the perspective of rated companies, exploring why firms continue to engage with ESG ratings despite criticism of their effectiveness, even as investors remain their primary users. Drawing on institutional theory, the authors adopt this underexplored perspective and investigate how ESG ratings become institutionalised within organisations. Design/methodology/approach Based on abductive thematic analysis of 45 semi-structured interviews with sustainability executives from listed European firms, the authors develop a framework distinguishing between substantive and symbolic forms of ESG rating institutionalisation. Findings ESG rating adoption is shaped by institutional pressures and unfolds along a continuum. At one end, firms substantively integrate sustainability considerations into core operations; at the other, ESG ratings are used symbolically to secure external recognition and legitimacy. This study also highlights the risk of deinstitutionalisation if the limitations of ESG ratings remain unaddressed. Practical implications This study offers managers, investors and policymakers insights into navigating ESG pressures and strengthening the credibility of ESG frameworks while providing a diagnostic lens to distinguish symbolic compliance from substantive integration. Social implications While the potential deinstitutionalisation of ESG ratings could erode credibility, accountability and investor trust, substantive adoption could benefit transparency, stakeholder oversight and the diffusion of sustainability norms. Addressing their limitations is therefore crucial for maintaining credibility in the financial sector and directing capital towards companies with meaningful sustainability practices. Originality/value This study extends research on corporate responses to ESG ratings by drawing on institutional theory and developing a conceptual framework of symbolic and substantive institutionalisation from the perspective of rated companies. Specifically, it shifts the explanatory focus beyond firms’ strategic orientations by showing that corporate responses are also shaped by the institutional characteristics and structural limitations of ESG rating systems, thereby advancing the concept of ESG ratings’ deinstitutionalisation.

title: INGENIERÍA ECONÓMICO-JURÍDICA, ACTUARIAL Y FINANCIERA DE SOCIEDADES POLICÉNTRICAS AUTÓNOMAS
summary: PROGRAMA/TESIS DOCTORAL INDEPENDIENTE Proyecto de investigación fundacional Arquitectura científica propuesta INGENIERÍA ECONÓMICO-JURÍDICA, ACTUARIAL Y FINANCIERA DE SOCIEDADES POLICÉNTRICAS AUTÓNOMAS Fundamentos para la transición hacia órdenes sociales privados, voluntarios, criptográficamente verificables, mutuales, cooperativos, industriales y patrimonialmente descentralizados. Subtítulo: Teoría de los polimonopolios endógenos multilocales, economías de capacidades, propiedad productiva, coordinación contractual y juegos evolutivos dinámicos endógenos volitivos. Objeto central: Construcción de un marco científico integral para estudiar las condiciones económicas, jurídicas, actuariales, financieras, tecnológicas e institucionales que permitirían la transición desde sociedades organizadas mediante monopolios territoriales de autoridad hacia sociedades de coordinación policéntrica, contractual, privada y voluntaria. Carácter de la investigación: Programa/Tesis doctoral independiente, interdisciplinar, teórico-analítica, matemático-institucional, propositiva y susceptible de contrastación empírica, no estrictamente austríaca, si tendientemente austríaca . Horizonte de investigación: 30 años. Ámbito de aplicación: Sistemas económicos locales, multilocales, industriales, digitales, transfronterizos y globales. Autoría: Fermín Ulaneo Fecha: Noviembre 2026. BLOQUE PRELIMINAR — PRESENTACIÓN Y FUNDAMENTOS DE LA INVESTIGACIÓN Este bloque comprende los elementos científicos, epistemológicos, metodológicos y conceptuales necesarios para establecer la identidad académica de la investigación. 1. Portada e identificación académica Título principal: Fundamentos para la transición hacia órdenes sociales privados Subtítulo científico: Teoría de los polimonopolios endógenos multilocales Naturaleza independiente de la investigación: Tesis doctoral independiente Autoría: Fermín Ulaneo. Fecha y lugar: Noviembre del 2026, España. Identificación institucional: No aplica. Clasificación científica: Interdisciplinar, teórico-analítica. Declaración de originalidad y trazabilidad documental: Susceptible de contrastación empírica. 2. Resumen ejecutivo de la investigación 2.1. Resumen general La investigación propone desarrollar una teoría integral de organización económica y jurídica basada en la coordinación voluntaria de individuos, empresas, propietarios, inventores, instituciones mutuales, organizaciones cooperativas y redes privadas de prestación de servicios. El objeto fundamental consiste en identificar, formalizar y evaluar las condiciones necesarias para constituir órdenes sociales capaces de coordinar producción, intercambio, financiación, protección patrimonial, resolución de conflictos, aseguramiento de riesgos, generación monetaria privada y provisión de infraestructuras sin depender estructuralmente de una autoridad territorial monopolística. La propuesta introduce una arquitectura institucional basada en siete elementos fundamentales: Policentrismo institucional: coexistencia de múltiples centros autónomos de decisión, contratación, financiación y prestación de servicios. Polimonopolios endógenos multilocales: organizaciones privadas que alcanzan posiciones de exclusividad económica mediante capacidades productivas, reputacionales, tecnológicas, contractuales y de coordinación, cuya continuidad depende de la aceptación voluntaria y de su capacidad para conservar clientes, capital y colaboradores. Mutualismo actuarial: agrupaciones voluntarias de personas y empresas para compartir riesgos mediante mecanismos de aseguramiento, reservas, reaseguro y distribución contractual de pérdidas. Propiedad productiva descentralizada: estructuras de propiedad, inversión, sucesión y capitalización capaces de multiplicar unidades productivas independientes. Infraestructuras monetarias y financieras privadas: sistemas de intercambio, liquidación, crédito, ahorro y financiación basados en reglas verificables y mecanismos competitivos. Resolución policéntrica de conflictos: instituciones especializadas en arbitraje, mediación, adjudicación y ejecución contractual. Juegos evolutivos dinámicos endógenos volitivos: una nueva arquitectura de análisis de decisiones estratégicas en la que los agentes pueden modificar preferencias, capacidades, compromisos, alianzas, reglas y estructuras de cooperación a lo largo del tiempo. La tesis no presupone que toda interacción económica sea necesariamente beneficiosa para todos los participantes. Investiga, por el contrario, bajo qué condiciones pueden transformarse conflictos distributivos, externalidades, incertidumbres y problemas de coordinación en procesos de creación conjunta de valor. El resultado esperado es una teoría institucional susceptible de formalización matemática, evaluación actuarial, análisis financiero, contrastación histórica y experimentación mediante simulaciones computacionales. 2.2. Abstract The research develops an interdisciplinary framework for the economic, legal, actuarial and financial foundations of polycentric voluntary societies. Its central objective is to investigate the institutional, technological and contractual conditions under which decentralized private organizations can provide economic coordination, insurance, monetary services, capital allocation, dispute resolution and productive infrastructure without relying on territorially monopolistic political authority. The proposed framework introduces endogenous multilocal poly-monopolies, voluntary mutual insurance architectures, decentralized productive ownership, private financial infrastructures, contractual governance and endogenous volitional evolutionary game theory. The research combines institutional economics, contract theory, mechanism design, actuarial mathematics, financial economics, cryptographic verification, evolutionary dynamics and industrial organization. Its principal scientific contribution is intended to be a formal and empirically testable architecture explaining how voluntary institutions emerge, compete, cooperate, adapt and reproduce across multiple geographical and technological environments. 2.3. Problema científico central ¿Cómo diseñar, financiar, asegurar, gobernar y reproducir sistemas sociales complejos en los que las funciones actualmente concentradas en instituciones territoriales monopolísticas puedan ser desarrolladas por redes autónomas, privadas, mutuales, cooperativas y contractuales? 2.4. Solución científica propuesta Desarrollar una arquitectura institucional multicapa que permita: Sustitución funcional progresiva de estructuras monopolísticas. Creación de organizaciones privadas de gobernanza. Desarrollo de sistemas monetarios competitivos. Provisión privada de servicios de protección, seguridad y justicia. Financiación industrial y tecnológica descentralizada. Aseguramiento mutual de riesgos sistémicos. Protección de derechos patrimoniales. Coordinación contractual entre jurisdicciones voluntarias. Expansión de las capacidades productivas humanas. Reducción de los costes de conflicto y cooperación. 2.5. Resultados y aportaciones esperadas La investigación aspira a producir: Una teoría económica de los polimonopolios endógenos. Una teoría actuarial de las sociedades mutuales autónomas. Una arquitectura jurídica de órdenes contractuales policéntricos. Un modelo financiero de capitalización institucional privada. Una teoría de transición monetaria sin banca central. Una teoría de transición institucional sin Estado. Una teoría evolutiva de cooperación y creación conjunta de valor. Un modelo cuantitativo de sostenibilidad intergeneracional. 3. Introducción general 3.1. Planteamiento del problema Las sociedades industriales contemporáneas concentran importantes funciones de coordinación económica, jurídica, monetaria, financiera y territorial en instituciones dotadas de facultades exclusivas. La investigación parte de una pregunta diferente: ¿Es posible desarrollar arquitecturas institucionales alternativas capaces de proporcionar esas mismas funciones, o funciones superiores, mediante organizaciones autónomas que compitan, cooperen, se especialicen y se coordinen voluntariamente? Esta pregunta requiere superar el tratamiento exclusivamente ideológico de la organización social. No basta con proponer la desaparición de una institución. Es necesario determinar: Qué funciones desempeña. Qué problemas resuelve. Qué incentivos sostienen su funcionamiento. Qué costes genera. Qué instituciones alternativas podrían asumir sus funciones. Qué mecanismos impedirían su captura. Cómo se financiarían. Cómo se asegurarían sus obligaciones. Cómo se resolverían los conflictos entre ellas. Cómo se produciría la transición sin provocar discontinuidades sistémicas. Por tanto, la abolición institucional, cuando sea objeto de la investigación, deberá estudiarse como un problema de sustitución funcional, no como una simple eliminación administrativa. 3.2. La unidad fundamental de análisis Se propone sustituir el análisis centrado exclusivamente en Estados, mercados nacionales y empresas individuales por una unidad institucional más amplia: La red autónoma de coordinación económico-jurídica. Esta unidad puede integrar: Individuos. Familias. Empresas. Cooperativas. Mutualidades. Aseguradoras. Organizaciones arbitrales. Redes de seguridad. Fondos de inversión. Instituciones monetarias. Plataformas tecnológicas. Organizaciones industriales. Redes de propietarios. Sistemas privados de acreditación y certificación. Cada organización constituye un agente institucional con recursos, capacidades, compromisos, derechos, obligaciones y mecanismos propios de adaptación. 3.3. Justificación de la investigación La investigación se justifica por la necesidad de integrar disciplinas que habitualmente estudian separadamente los problemas de organización social. Disciplina

title: ESG Disclosure, Profitability, Current Ratio, and Company Value in Indonesian Energy Companies
summary: Background: The growing importance of sustainable finance has widened the information set used in corporate valuation. This is particularly relevant for Indonesian energy firms, whose market performance is shaped by a combination of environmental exposure, capital intensity, and near-term financial capacity. Objective: This study assesses whether ESG disclosure, profitability, and liquidity are statistically associated with firm value among energy-sector issuers on the Indonesia Stock Exchange during 2023–2025. Methods: A panel-data design was applied to 90 firm-year observations from 30 energy companies selected purposively from 91 listed firms. The analysis used annual financial statements and sustainability reports. ESG disclosure was scored against the GRI Standards 2021, profitability was measured by Return on Assets (ROA), liquidity by the Current Ratio (CR), and firm value by Price to Book Value (PBV). Panel estimation was performed in EViews 12, with specification testing indicating the use of company fixed effects. Results: In the fixed-effects regression, ESG disclosure was positively associated with PBV (coefficient = 3.379502; p = 0.0158). ROA also showed a positive association (coefficient = 0.019785; p = 0.0049), as did CR (coefficient = 0.265845; p < 0.001). The model was significant overall and produced an adjusted R² of 0.804446. Conclusion: The evidence from the observed firms indicates that sustainability disclosure and financial fundamentals are jointly relevant to market valuation. Higher ESG disclosure, profitability, and liquidity were each accompanied by higher PBV, although the non-experimental panel design permits association-based rather than causal interpretation.

title: HUMAN-CENTRIC DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION AND HRM INNOVATION: EXPLORING THE FUTURE OF WORKFORCE MANAGEMENT IN TECHNOLOGY-DRIVEN ORGANIZATIONS
summary: Artificial intelligence AI, automation, people analytics, and integrated digital platforms are transforming human resource management (HRM). This narrative review explores the impact of these technologies on HRM and suggests principles for effective, human-centric HRM innovation. It brings together conceptual, empirical, and policy literature on digital recruitment, workforce analytics, development of employees, hybrid working, algorithmic management, and ethical governance. The reviewed evidence suggests that digital HRM has the potential to enhance efficiency in HR administration, recruitment assistance, workforce planning, learning, and flexibility at work. These benefits are contingent on the quality of the data, readiness of the organization, a proper work design, and employee involvement. Issues such as algorithmic bias, intrusive monitoring, privacy risks, inequitable access to digital skills, and decreased autonomy for employees are still significant issues. Evidence for AI-supported work tasks and hybrid work has been found in certain contexts but not universally in other work contexts or organizations. The review suggests an integrated solution of strategic alignment, human-centered work design, workforce capability development, responsible technology governance, and continuous performance evaluation. Along with organizational performance, there are centerpiece evaluation criteria that focus on employee well-being, fairness, transparency, trust, and human oversight. The suggested approach is a conceptual model that does not validate the sustainable workforce management approach through empirical evidence. It necessitates consistently auditing, having an easily accessible grievance procedure, training and retaining diverse employees, and communicating with employees in a transparent manner. Longitudinal, comparative, and intervention studies in a variety of organizational settings should be used to evaluate long-term effects in future research.

title: Impact of Digital Leadership on Digital Transformation Readiness in MSMEs: A Review
summary: The contemporary business environment is characterised by unprecedented volatility, uncertainty, complexity, and ambiguity (VUCA), making digital transformation readiness a strategic imperative for Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) that constitute over 90% of all businesses globally and employ approximately 60–70% of the workforce. This conceptual review paper examines the impact of digital leadership on digital transformation readiness in MSMEs, with particular focus on Nigeria and Kano State. The main aim is to synthesise existing theoretical and empirical evidence and develop an integrated conceptual framework positioning the three dimensions of digital leadership digital vision and strategic foresight, technological enablement and dynamic capabilities, and innovation facilitation and empowerment as antecedents of digital transformation readiness comprising technological readiness, organisational readiness, and environmental readiness. The study adopted a systematic conceptual review design following adapted PRISMA guidelines, searching eight academic databases (Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, EBSCOhost, Emerald Insight, ScienceDirect, JSTOR, and ProQuest) for the period January 2015 to December 2025. The review integrated dynamic capabilities theory (Teece, 2007), transformational leadership theory (Bass & Avolio, 1994), and technology-organisation-environment (TOE) framework (Tornatzky & Fleischer, 1990) into a unified framework adapted to Nigerian and Kano contexts. Policymakers (SMEDAN, Kano State Enterprise Development Agency) should design training addressing all three dimensions and address infrastructural deficits through solar-powered digital hubs. Development organisations should reallocate resources toward innovation empowerment given high failure rates. The framework offers eighteen testable propositions to guide future empirical research in resource-constrained environments.

title: Climate Resilience and Smart Community Governance Through Digital Transformation
summary: This research has investigated the concept of digital transformation as a way to build climate resilience and smart community governance. In particular, this study sought to explore the ways in which digital technology, data-driven decision-making, intelligent infrastructures, and participatory governance can help communities prepare for, respond to, and recover from climate risks. In this regard, qualitative and conceptual research approach has been used in order to identify relevant concepts of climate resilience, smart community, digital governance, sustainability, and community participation. Technologies that may contribute to climate risk assessment, resource management, emergency response, and community planning such as artificial intelligence, IoT, big data analytics, cloud computing, digital platforms, and geographic information systems have been considered in the analysis. This research has developed a conceptual framework that incorporates climate risk assessment, digital data gathering, intelligent analysis, smart infrastructures, stakeholder participation, adaptive governance, and continuous monitoring into an organized resilience process. In addition, special attention was paid to transparency, inclusiveness, accessibility, data security, privacy, and human-centered decision-making in digital transformation. According to the research, digital transformation can serve as an integrative platform for addressing climate risks, coordination of institutions, evidence-based governance, and increasing community resilience. The framework highlighted that the use of technology should supplement but not substitute human thinking, institutional accountability, and community engagement. The research made a contribution to the formation of a conceptual basis for the combination of digital transformation and climate-resilient/smart community governance.

title: Buyer green innovation volatility and the supplier bullwhip effect: a signalling theory perspective
summary: Purpose Buyers' green innovation does not remain confined within the firm; its volatility may ripple upstream and reshape suppliers' operations. Drawing on signalling theory, we examine how buyers' green innovation volatility (GIV) affects the supplier bullwhip effect (SBE), and how buyers' green supplier management (GSM) and inventory utilisation efficiency (IUE) moderate this effect. Design/methodology/approach We construct a dyadic dataset covering 436 Chinese buyer firms and 871 global suppliers from 2012 to 2022, and employ fixed-effects models to test our hypotheses. Findings There is a U-shaped GIV–SBE relationship: compared with both low and high levels of GIV, moderate GIV leads suppliers to adjust production more cautiously in response to unstable demand, resulting in lower SBE. When buyers' green innovation is on an overall downward trend, GSM helps suppliers interpret demand and operational changes more accurately, curbing GIV-induced increases in SBE. Higher IUE enables suppliers to detect GIV-related requirement changes more promptly, prompting stronger production responses and widening the SBE gap between moderate and low or high GIV. Originality/value By introducing GIV, our study identifies a novel antecedent of SBE and provides insights into how buyers can help suppliers accurately interpret GIV and calibrate their operational responses.

title: IMPROVING REVENUE RECOGNITION UNDER INTERNATIONAL FINANCIAL REPORTING STANDARDS IN CONSTRUCTION CONTRACTING ORGANIZATIONS.
summary: The article examines the issues of aligning the procedure for revenue recognition in construction contracting organizations of Uzbekistan with the requirements of International Financial Reporting Standard (IFRS) 15 "Revenue from Contracts with Customers". The five-step model of IFRS 15, the criteria for satisfying a performance obligation over time, the methods of measuring the stage of completion (the input and output methods), variable consideration, contract modifications, and the presentation of contract assets and contract liabilities are considered. Practical problems arising in the transition from National Accounting Standards (NAS) to IFRS are identified, and proposals for resolving them are developed. A hypothetical numerical example is provided for the analysis. The results contribute to increasing the transparency and international comparability of the financial statements of construction organizations.

title: Processing capacity under complexity: an organizational information processing perspective on humanitarian supply chain performance
summary: Purpose This study aims to investigate the role of processing capacity in shaping humanitarian supply chain performance under crisis conditions. Specifically, it examines how information processing capacity influences response performance and equity performance, and how environmental complexity and structural integration moderate these relationships. It also examines whether environmental complexity moderates the information processing capacity-equity performance relationship more strongly than the information processing capacity-response performance relationship. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on Organizational Information Processing Theory (OIPT) and a contingency perspective, the research model is proposed and empirically evaluated using survey data collected from 600 professionals with relevant experience working in the humanitarian supply chain across India. The hypotheses were tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS. Findings The PLS-SEM results show that processing capacity has a significant positive effect on both response performance and equity performance. The environmental complexity amplifies the impact of processing capacity on both outcomes, but results confirm that it has stronger moderating effect for equity performance compared to response performance. Similarly, structural integration also significantly strengthens the relationship positively between processing capacity and both performance dimensions. Research limitations/implications First, this study extends OIPT to humanitarian supply chains by demonstrating that the relationship between information processing capacity and performance depends on environmental complexity. Second, it advances contingency-based reasoning by showing that environmental complexity strengthens the relationship between processing capacity and equity performance more than its relationship with response performance, suggesting that the value of processing capacity varies across humanitarian performance dimensions. Third, it extends OIPT by identifying structural integration, defined as the alignment between emergency and routine supply chain structures, as an organizational condition that strengthens the relationship between processing capacity and both response and equity performance. Practical implications The results and analysis presented in the study suggest that humanitarian organizations need to prioritize coordination among multiple actors, real-time information sharing, decentralized decision-making, and structural integration explained through the mechanisms of emergency and routine supply chain tasks. Originality/value This study contributes to the humanitarian supply chain literature by theorizing and empirically showing that processing capacity matters differently across humanitarian performance dimensions. It demonstrates that environmental complexity strengthens the processing capacity-performance relationship more strongly for equity performance than for response performance. The study also shows that structural integration enables humanitarian organizations to translate processing capacity into improved response and equity outcomes.

title: The Moderating and Joint Effects of Firm Size on Corporate Governance and Financial Performance: Empirical Evidence from Construction and Allied Firms Listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange
summary: To support Kenya’s Bottom-up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA), listed construction and allied firms receive substantial resources for national infrastructure projects, despite persistent operational and financial challenges. This study examined the moderating and joint effects of firm size on the relationship between corporate governance characteristics and financial performance among construction and allied firms listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE). Using a ten-year panel regression framework, the study tested hypotheses on firm size as a moderator and joint predictor alongside directors’ remuneration, board composition, and board meetings. The study was anchored on Agency, Stakeholder, and Firm Characteristics theories and adopted a descriptive longitudinal design, inferential statistics, and a census of four listed firms. Bamburi Cement PLC, Crown Paints Kenya PLC, East African Cables PLC, and East African Portland Cement PLC. Secondary panel data spanning ten years from 2015 to 2024 were gathered from audited financial statements using a structured secondary checklist and analysed using STATA Version 18. The moderated panel regression model yielded a statistically significant overall fit ) with an overall coefficient of determination ( ) of 39.84%. The interaction term between directors' remuneration and firm size was positive and statistically insignificant at the 5% p-level ( , ), indicating that larger asset scale exacerbates the positive profitability impact of unaligned executive compensation. The null hypothesis was not rejected. The joint multivariate regression model demonstrated statistical significance , ) with an overall of 33.976%. Directors' remuneration ( , ) and board meeting frequency ( , ) maintained significant negative direct relationships, while firm size exerted a significant B positive scale advantage ( , ). The null hypothesis was rejected. Firm size significantly moderates and jointly influences financial performance, requiring governance practices, compensation, and meeting frequencies tailored to scale.

title: Foundry Operations in Unified Supply Chain Digital Twins: A Cross-Industry Literature Review
summary: Abstract The foundry industry is among the industries with the highest potential for digitalization, and occupies a critical, intermediate position in the industrial value chain, supplying cast components to the automotive, machinery, infrastructure, and energy sectors. To unlock this potential and enable cross-industry interoperability, digital twins (DTs) offer a promising approach for minimizing time, costs, and environmental impacts. This exploratory scoping review maps the existing literature on each pillar of the idea and calls for further research on this topic. The aim of this paper is to explore the existing literature, identify the problems, and discuss what research is necessary to address them from a holistic perspective. The methods are explained in three main topics: (i) scope of existing research, (ii) literature-based maturity assessment models for DTs, and (iii) specific methods employed in current studies. This review identifies key themes in the results, including methods for measuring digital twin maturity, current initiatives, and reference frameworks, interoperable data spaces, and available modeling software. The subsequent discussion addresses the challenges of advancing DT maturity and achieving cross-sector interoperability, the semantic, technical, and governance requirements that follow for foundry DTs, and the challenges that interoperable DTs can address, drawing on the reviewed initiatives, maturity models, and application cases from the foundry industry and from neighboring industries such as mining. The review answers four research questions on the challenges of the foundry industry, on DT maturity models, on interoperability initiatives and applications, and on the requirements for foundry digital twins. It collects the evidence from the literature for the view that the foundry industry is a digital bottleneck in the supply chains of cast products without testing it, and highlights the resulting research gaps. Ultimately, this work provides a structured review and a research agenda that reduces ambiguity and outlines future standardization efforts and research directions toward sustainable, digitalized foundry operations.

title: Selecting the right path: a framework for lead-time reduction in consumer goods supply chains
summary: Purpose Consumer goods firms often face severe shortages caused by forecast inaccuracy, where a few variants become unexpected bestsellers and trigger costly stockouts. This article positions the choice of lead-time reduction initiatives as a crucial decision for enhancing responsiveness and mitigating shortages and frames this decision as a performance-management prioritization problem under uncertainty. Design/methodology/approach This work developed a pragmatic direction-selection framework grounded in a design science approach and applied in a case to guide managers in evaluating and prioritizing lead-time reduction initiatives. The framework integrates insights from the literature with feasibility-oriented evaluation criteria, applying the principles of multi-criteria decision analysis to assess initiatives in terms of expected return on investment (impact relative to effort) and implementation horizon. Findings The study offers a theory-based, empirically validated framework for identifying and planning lead time reduction initiatives in a context of hard-to-predict demand, making explicit a performance-management logic for prioritizing responsiveness initiatives. The case shows that initiatives with attractive expected impact–effort profiles are not necessarily robust priorities once implementation risk and sensitivity to assumptions are considered. Research limitations/implications The study advances performance-management research by reframing lead-time reduction as a decision problem under uncertainty and extending the focus from performance evaluation to intervention selection, translating dispersed responsiveness insights into a replicable prioritization logic, validated in a real case and supported by sensitivity checks. Practical implications The study provides a stepwise decision-support tool that helps cross-functional teams prioritize feasible lead-time reduction initiatives and translate them into an implementation plan, with risk and sensitivity checks to avoid assumption-driven choices. Originality/value The paper offers a validated innovative decision-support framework that operationalizes lead-time reduction as a performance-management choice under demand uncertainty, using an explicit prioritization logic to select responsiveness initiatives end-to-end.

title: Green Value Investing in the Banking Sector: The Effectiveness of a Green F-Score Strategy in Poland as a CEE Case Study
summary: The banking sector serves as a critical transmission belt for capital allocation toward renewable energy (RE) projects, yet traditional equity valuation models fail to capture banks' exposure to energy transition risks. To bridge this gap, this paper develops a novel fundamental-environmental indicator—the "Green F-Score"—tested on 10 major commercial banks listed on the Warsaw Stock Exchange (WSE) between 2023 and 2025. By synthesizing classical financial efficiency criteria with EU Taxonomy disclosures (Green Asset Ratio), the portfolio sorting methodology reveals how capital markets price sustainable energy financing in Central and Eastern Europe. The empirical results demonstrate that portfolios with high environmental-fundamental readiness ("Green Leaders") generate a superior mean annual return of 60.43% and a substantial price-to-book (P/B) premium. Conversely, banks lagging in RE financing suffer significant carbon risk discounts. Correlation analysis confirms a paradigm shift: the market premium is primarily driven by the ESG sub-score, rendering traditional financial metrics a mere operational hygiene factor. Consequently, the Green F-Score emerges as a robust tool for institutional investors, proving that accelerated lending to the energy transition effectively lowers the cost of equity capital for commercial banks.

title: Hospital logistics in Somalia: why health-specific supply chain expertise matters—an opinion
summary: Hospital logistics determines whether care promised on paper can actually be delivered at the bedside. A hospital may have trained clinicians and functioning wards, yet treatment can still fail when oxygen interfaces, essential medicines, sterile supplies, laboratory reagents, blood-bank consumables, or device accessories are unavailable. In Somalia, this issue deserves greater policy attention because the health system operates under financial constraints, import dependence, insecurity, fragmented service delivery, and uneven institutional capacity. Somalia's Health Sector Strategic Plan 2022-2026 describes important pharmaceutical-sector challenges and a private pharmacy logistics network that, although rapid, operates largely through informal and trust-based processes without formal forecasting or contracting arrangements (1).In a WHO report on Somalia's 2020 pharmaceutical-sector assessment, stock-outs averaged 27.3 days per year in surveyed public health centres and warehouses (2). Although this finding should not be generalized to all Somali health facilities, it illustrates the operational vulnerabilities affecting pharmaceutical availability. Research examining Somalia's humanitarian health response has also documented recurrent procurement and transport-related shortages affecting medicines and other essential health commodities (3). Recent Somalia-focused health-systems commentary has additionally highlighted severe health-workforce scarcity, weak regulation, uneven deployment, and financing instability as threats to continuity and resilience of health services (4). These observations are not evidence that all Somali hospitals experience the same logistics weaknesses or that existing logistics personnel are ineffective. Rather, they expose a broader healthpolicy question: whether hospital logistics is best treated mainly as a generic administrative function or as a specialized health-system capability requiring competencies specific to medicines, medical devices, clinical demand, quality assurance, and patient safety. In this Opinion, health-specific supply-chain expertise refers to the combination of conventional supply-chain competencies with sufficient technical knowledge of medicines, medical devices, diagnostics, medical gases, storage and quality requirements, and the clinical consequences of procurement and inventory decisions.Generic supply-chain competence remains essential. Procurement planning, tendering, supplier management, inventory control, warehousing, transportation, budgeting, and contract management all matter. Health care, however, introduces technical requirements that substantially change the consequences of purchasing decisions. Ordering an unsuitable office product may create inconvenience; purchasing an incompatible ventilator circuit, an inappropriate oxygen regulator, a reagent without a compatible analyzer, a medicine with insufficient remaining shelf life, or equipment that cannot be maintained locally may interrupt treatment and waste scarce resources. Somalia's Essential Medicines List is intended to guide procurement, management, distribution, and regulation of medicines while supporting standardized medical care (5). Translating such guidance into hospital purchasing decisions requires more than comparing prices and delivery times. Supply-chain personnel must understand clinical consumption patterns, dosage forms and strengths, storage conditions, substitution risks, expiry management, cold-chain requirements, infection-prevention specifications, regulatory requirements, and the relationship between equipment and the consumables required to keep it functional.The international health-supply-chain literature increasingly recognizes the workforce itself as a core health-system resource. A recent professionalization framework emphasizes defined competencies, standardized job descriptions, education pathways, and career structures for health supply-chain personnel (6). Related work argues that reliable health supply chains depend on a competent, supported, and recognized workforce rather than ad hoc assignment of supply-chain responsibilities (7). Evidence from Ghana, Rwanda, and Uganda similarly demonstrates the importance of supply-chain competencies, dedicated roles, organizational support, and functional logistics information systems (8)(9)(10). Although these studies come from other settings, they provide a transferable framework for considering which competencies may be relevant to Somali hospitals; local adaptation and evaluation remain necessary.Health-specific supply-chain expertise does not require every logistician to become a physician, nurse, or pharmacist. Nor does it imply that already overburdened clinicians need to operate procurement departments and warehouses. A potentially appropriate model is a professional health supply-chain function that combines modern supply-chain expertise with sufficient understanding of health products and formal collaboration with clinical, pharmacy, laboratory, biomedical, finance, and infection-prevention teams.At minimum, hospital supply-chain personnel would benefit from the capability to translate service activity into quantification and forecasting; distinguish essential from discretionary products; verify technical specifications; evaluate suppliers beyond price; manage batch, expiry, temperature, and traceability requirements; calculate reorder levels and buffer stocks; identify single-source vulnerabilities; and use logistics data for management decisions. Purchases carrying substantial clinical or technical risk would warrant review by the relevant professional department.Medical equipment illustrates why this distinction matters. A systematic review of medical-device procurement in low-and middle-income countries found that equipment selection is better informed by infrastructure, end-user capability, maintenance requirements, and life-cycle costs rather than acquisition price alone (11). WHO health-technology-management guidance similarly places procurement within a continuum extending through incoming inspection, inventory, user training, maintenance, performance monitoring, and eventual decommissioning (12). For Somali hospitals, purchasing a monitor, ventilator, anesthesia machine, oxygen system, or laboratory analyzer would therefore benefit from assessment of electricity requirements, compatibility, spare parts, consumables, end-user training, preventive maintenance, technical support, and replacement planning. Hospitals can begin this transition without creating a large new bureaucracy. First, hospitals could define a health supply-chain competency profile for personnel responsible for procurement, stores, inventory, and internal distribution.Recruitment and promotion could assess these competencies, while existing staff could be offered structured professional development through short courses, postgraduate education, certification, mentorship, and continuing professional development. Although addressing disaster and emergencycare education rather than supply-chain management specifically, recent Somali commentary has similarly emphasized profession-specific competencies, explicit learning objectives, interprofessional coordination, and adaptation of training to resource-constrained environments (13). These principles may be relevant to building a competent hospital supply-chain workforce in Somalia.Second, hospitals could establish multidisciplinary procurement and supply oversight with clear thresholds for technical review. Routine low-risk commodities can remain administratively streamlined, whereas medicines, medical gases, high-risk consumables, diagnostics, and medical devices could undergo pharmacy, clinical, laboratory, biomedical, infection-prevention, or other relevant technical review as appropriate. Such an approach preserves the essential role of logistics and finance personnel while reducing the probability of technically unsuitable purchases.Third, logistics-management information can function as a management instrument rather than merely a record-keeping requirement. A minimum hospital supply-chain performance set could be grouped into four domains: availability (stock-out days, order fill rate, and emergency purchases); efficiency (forecast accuracy, supplier lead time, and inventory turnover); quality and safety (expiry and wastage, traceability, and equipment downtime); and resilience (qualified alternative suppliers and critical-item contingency plans). Persistent logistics failures can then be reviewed alongside clinical quality and patient-safety indicators because commodity shortages may directly undermine care.For emergency preparedness, structured stockpiling may also strengthen continuity. The 5P Strategic Medical Stockpile model integrates stockpile planning within the emergency-management cycle and offers a conceptual reference for emergency buffers, alternative supply arrangements, and replenishment planning, although adaptation to the Somali context would be required (14).Fourth, procurement decisions could place greater emphasis on total value rather than unit price alone. For medicines and consumables, value includes quality, shelf life, regulatory compliance, storage requirements, and delivery reliability. For medical devices, it includes installation, compatibility, consumables, spare parts, warranties, training, maintenance, and expected useful life. In resourceconstrained hospitals, the lowest-priced item may ultimately be the most expensive if it cannot be safely used or kept functional.Finally, hospitals, universities, and health authorities could increasingly recognize health supplychain management as a legitimate professional and educational pathway. Somalia needs personnel who understand both supply-chain science and the health-service consequences of logistics decisions. Specialized postgraduate education, competency-based in-service programs, and multidisciplinary training involving logisticians, pharmacists, nurses, physicians, biomedical professionals, finance teams, and hospital managers could help build this capability. The objective is professionalization, not professional displacement.Strengthening hospital logistics in Somalia is not principally about changing job titles. It is about improving the governance of decisions that determine whether essential inputs reach patients in the correct form, quality, quantity, condition, and time. Generic logistics expertise remains indispensable, but hospitals manage products for which procurement and supply errors can cause immediate clinical harm, service interruption, financial waste, or unusable technology. This additional risk justifies healthspecific competency standards and multidisciplinary technical oversight.The policy direction is therefore practical rather than prescriptive. Somali hospitals could recognize health supply-chain management as a specialized clinical-support function, define competency-based roles, integrate technical review into high-risk procurement, use logistics data in executive decisionmaking, and develop formal education and career pathways. National health authorities, universities, hospitals, professional organizations, and development partners can facilitate this transition by aligning curricula, job descriptions, procurement standards, and performance indicators. Somalia does not need to replace existing logistics systems or personnel to pursue this agenda. It can strengthen them by ensuring that supply-chain decisions incorporate the technical realities of healthcare delivery. In a health system where every scarce resource must generate maximum patient benefit, professionalizing hospital supply chains can be viewed as an investment in safer, more reliable, and more resilient health services.

title: Digital Transformation and Business Portfolio Reconfiguration: Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation
summary: Digital conversion is re-understanding the limits between telecommunications, media, and entertainment sectors, presenting new chances for well-established telecom companies to broaden their operations outside of traditional connectivity offerings. This research probes into the relationship between digital transition and business portfolio enhancement via a case analysis of Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation (NTT). Based on the theories regarding dynamic capabilities, digital business model innovation, and platform ecosystems, this study shows how NTT employs its network infrastructure, customer communication channels, and data resources to organize entertainment-related services. The analysis pinpoints four beneficial operating mechanisms: accessing end-customers through communication services, achieving personalized service backed by data, creating superior entertainment experiences enabled by technologies, and facilitating integrated service transactions. In the meantime, four significant challenges are found. There is competition over resources between the telecom and entertainment sectors. Disputes emerge in organizational frameworks and corporate cultures. The company depends significantly on external content suppliers, and its business portfolio becomes overly diversified. This research proposes several solutions, such as cross-business cooperation frameworks, combined units for technological and content innovation, graded portfolio management, inter-departmental performance assessment systems, and enhanced data governance. The study reaches the conclusion that sustainable value generation cannot be accomplished solely via technology investment. Enterprises are required to dynamically integrate digital capabilities, organizational resources, and portfolio strategies within a unified ecosystem.

title: Digital Transformation Processes in Large Infrastructure Owners: An Organizational Change Perspective
summary: Abstract Large infrastructure owners (LIOs) own and operate the critical infrastructure that underpins modern society. Under growing demands for efficiency and resilience, digital transformation (DT) entailing both technological and organizational change has become a strategic necessity for LIOs to sustain service delivery. The change process of DT in LIOs unfolds under the competing demands of digital initiatives and high-reliability operations, which converge on organizational members expected to enact the initiatives while upholding uninterrupted services. However, existing studies on DT in LIOs have concentrated on technology adoption, and broader DT process research leaves unexplained how members come to enact transformation. To address these gaps, this study focuses on the internal change process of DT in LIOs, examining how organizational strategies deepen member engagement across stages. Adopting an organizational change lens and a cross-level process framework that spans organizational and individual levels, we trace how organizations reshape established arrangements to bring members into DT. Through a single-case study of a Chinese airport group, we identify three stage-specific strategic mechanisms: establishing legitimacy under authoritative leadership, enacting safety-first logics in technology and organizing, and embedding identity change among members. A member-centric process model is then abstracted, conceptualizing DT progression as a recursive process advanced through deepening member engagement under specific contextual conditions. This study contributes to research on DT in LIOs by delineating how they sequence and adapt their strategies to realize systemic DT, enriches the broader DT literature by tracing DT progression through member engagement, and advances organizational change research by elucidating the recursive interplay between strategies and member responses that sustains DT as continuous change. Practically, advancing DT in LIOs requires drawing legitimacy and capabilities from outside the organization, while deriving opportunities from continuous operations and creating authorized space for digital work within them.

title: Digital Transformation, Teaching Strategies, Critical Thinking, and Mathematics and Science Education
summary: This issue focuses on digital transformation, teaching strategies, critical thinking, mathematics education, science education, and several additional topics. We begin with four articles on digital transformation. The articles examine Xuexitong for English learning, a component-based model of students' readiness to engage with digital platforms, the use of educational technology to enhance student performance in an English for Academic Purposes course, and the effectiveness of a distance teaching practicum program. Then, we present three articles on teaching strategies. The articles explore feminist pedagogy, the flipped classroom model, integration of humour into the classroom, and teacher effectiveness. We then share three articles on critical thinking. They investigate the Critical Thinking Assessment Scale-Short Form, embedding fiction in case studies within a non-literature course, and critical thinking skills. We continue with three articles on mathematics education. The articles examine integration of digital manipulatives in early childhood mathematics, Indonesia’s Pancasila Learner Profile Strengthening Project, and student achievement. Then we present three articles on science education. They include articles on the effectiveness of guided inquiry, the impact of augmented reality learning, and the links between ethnoscience, science literacy, and digital literacy. We also present articles on race and racism, entrepreneurship education, professional learning communities, and academic calling. This issue includes two dialogue and commentary articles on Generative AI and large language models, concluding with four book reviews.

title: AI AND CORPORATE GOVERNANCE IN INDIA: EXAMINING DIRECTORS' DUTIES, FIDUCIARY RESPONSIBILITIES AND LIABILITY FOR AI-ASSISTED DECISIONS
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support corporate decisions involving finance, compliance, recruitment, risk assessment, cybersecurity and business strategy. These tools can improve speed and help directors process large amounts of information, but they can also produce inaccurate, biased or difficult-to-explain recommendations. This creates a central corporate-law question: when a director relies on an AI-generated recommendation, does that reliance satisfy the director's existing legal duties, and who should be accountable if the decision causes harm? This paper examines the question through a doctrinal and comparative legal method. It analyses the Companies Act, 2013, particularly section 166, relevant principles emerging from Indian decisions on directors' fiduciary obligations and oversight and selected regulatory approaches to AI governance. It argues that Indian company law already provides a meaningful foundation for accountability through duties of good faith, care, diligence, independent judgment and avoidance of conflicts of interest. Those duties do not disappear when a company uses technology. However, the application of traditional standards to opaque or probabilistic AI systems raises practical questions about reasonable reliance, explainability, documentation and board-level supervision. The paper recommends a proportionate, risk-based approach: directors should not be strictly liable merely because an AI-assisted decision fails, but they should be expected to understand material risks, test important outputs, preserve meaningful human judgment and ensure appropriate oversight. The aim should be responsible innovation rather than either unrestricted automation or a blanket prohibition on AI-assisted governance.

title: Preventing Corporate Disputes Through Family Settlements: An Interdisciplinary Analysis of Family Law and Corporate Governance in India
summary: Family-owned businesses play a significant role in India, but when matters of succession, ownership, and/or management of the business become corporate disputes, the continuity of the family business is threatened. Family settlements are a recognised way to settle disputes about family property and multiple claims, but their utility as tools for preventing disputes has been relatively underdeveloped in the context of family-owned businesses. This article aims to explore whether family settlements can serve as a governance mechanism to prevent potential family conflicts within family-owned businesses. It examines the legal principles applicable to family settlements and their application in Kale v Deputy Director of Consolidation and Ram Charan Das v Girja Nandini Devi and their interplay with the Companies Act, 2013 and corporate governance. A carefully drafted family settlement sets clear expectations regarding succession provisions, co-ownership, involvement in management, shareholder voting on decisions, and resolution mechanisms for disputes within the family. Such settlements, however, cannot replace the mandatory corporate law, the company's constitution, or the rights of non-family shareholders. The article thus urges a perspective of family settlements as an additional layer of family governance, which can contribute to resolving family conflicts before they reach the level of corporate litigation. The article shows how to integrate family law concepts into corporate governance, thereby proposing to avoid conflict and controversy within the family business by establishing structured and forward-looking agreements.

title: The Effect of Technology Utilization, Internal Control Systems, and Environmental Costs on Financial Reporting Quality
summary: Financial reporting quality is essential for ensuring transparency, accountability, and the reliability of financial information in hospital management. However, the extent to which technology utilization, internal control systems, and environmental cost management contribute to financial reporting quality requires further empirical examination. This study aims to analyze the effects of technology utilization, internal control systems, and environmental costs on financial reporting quality at Rosela Hospital, Karawang, Indonesia. A quantitative approach was employed using a questionnaire-based survey involving employees in finance, accounting, and administration selected through purposive sampling. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS. The findings indicate that technology utilization and internal control systems do not have statistically significant effects on financial reporting quality, whereas environmental costs have a positive and significant effect. These results suggest that the availability of technology and internal control mechanisms alone may not be sufficient to improve financial reporting quality, while appropriate environmental cost management can contribute to more comprehensive and accountable financial information. This study concludes that hospitals should strengthen the identification, classification, recording, and reporting of environmental costs as part of their financial management practices. The practical impact of this research is to provide insights for hospital management into improving financial accountability and developing more transparent reporting practices. The findings should be interpreted in the context of the study’s limited scope, which focuses on a single hospital.
